items.title: Hollywood Needs a New Pixar
items.description: H ollywood earned its cultural monopoly by absorbing radical technologies that it first resisted: sound, color, computer graphics. People in the industry initially feared that Pixar’s computer animation would replace human actors with “digital doubles.” Similarly, most of the conversation about AI today revolves around cost savings and artist displacement. These issues are important, but they miss an even bigger shift that AI is accelerating. Ask a teenager where their favorite characters come from, and the answer is as likely to be a creator platform—YouTube, Roblox, TikTok—as a Hollywood studio. Unless moviemakers evolve, they risk losing their place at the center of culture. Those who combine new technology with storytelling, and who bring audiences into the creative process, will define the next century of entertainment. Silicon Valley and Hollywood went through a version of this before, during the early partnership between Pixar and Disney that was crucial to Pixar’s success. Disney storytellers gave Pixar pointed feedback on early Pixar characters, leading John Lasseter, Pete Docter, and the rest of the brain trust to take screenwriting classes. Pixar didn’t believe that technical people were any less creative than artists. Every discipline mattered. The result: Toy Story . Disney didn’t produce Toy Story by hiring more CGI artists into its 2-D pipeline. Instead, it partnered with Pixar, whose mission was to make movies with the new technology, and eventually acquired it. Pixar had tech that worked, artists who were intimate with it, and a culture of mutual admiration among its artistic and technological creators. Disney had marketing, distribution, major capital, logistical know-how, and a glorious legacy. Neither could build what the other had. Something similar needs to happen now. Hollywood has an opportunity to partner with studios built for AI, but the rise of creator culture will make the transition harder. During the shift to computer animation and graphics in the 1980s and ’90s, the distribution formats stayed the same—theaters, home video, and broadcast. Today, format, distribution, and production technology are changing all at once. [ Read: The corner of Hollywood that’s most susceptible to AI ] YouTube made more than $60 billion last year, about $15 billion more than Netflix brought in. To keep up, Hollywood studios are adapting properties from creator platforms. They found success with Backrooms (which cost about $10 million to make but collected more than $400 million at the box office) and Obsession (less than $1 million to make; more than $520 million at the box office), and are now rushing to find more YouTube properties and talent. Though this is smart, these audiences were formed and cultivated on other platforms. The Minecraft movie made almost $1 billion, a fraction of the game franchise’s $10 to $12 billion. The movie was effectively a marketing event for the game. AI didn’t cause the shift to creator platforms, but it will accelerate it. MrBeast, who has more than 500 million YouTube subscribers, built an empire without AI, but the technology allows would-be creators to realize their visions, and it enables existing creators to work more efficiently. But what about the ethics of using AI models that were trained on artists’ work without their permission or payment? Artists should be compensated for the work that was used to train models. These issues need to be settled in court and through regulation and licensing. The technology won’t go away, so we need artists to help set its terms. But rejecting AI altogether is not the answer. Across Asia, creators face many of the same concerns, but the technological and cultural shift is further along. In China, microdramas —scripted series typically filmed in portrait mode and designed for smartphone viewing, with episodes lasting one to three minutes—have compressed the distance between creation, distribution, and monetization; generative AI fits naturally into an industrial ecosystem built around rapid iteration, low production costs, and huge volumes of content. In Korea, webtoons and web novels move across streaming, games, music, and other formats. In India, a multilingual audience creates especially strong incentives for AI-assisted dubbing. It is a misperception that creators in the Global South care less about copyright, labor costs, or artistic integrity—if anything, Asia’s creator industries are quickly converging with the West on these questions. The difference is that much of the experimentation is happening within entertainment industries that have been more entrepreneurial and are more willing to embrace new technology. The first “ Toy Story moment” for both AI and the new formats it enables—a work whose artistic and cultural appeal makes the technology itself almost beside the point—may not be far away. The companies and countries that achieve it first could change perceptions of AI in creative work and accrue outsize cultural reach. In that sense, the U.S.-China technology competition is also becoming a competition over who builds the tools, platforms, and creative communities that shape global culture. H ollywood has defined mainstream culture for a century, and storytelling remains its greatest asset. However, treating YouTube, Roblox, and TikTok as farm systems to feed traditional distribution misses that audiences are on the farm. Netflix recently laid off 1,000 employees; Disney laid off roughly 1,500 this year and has said more layoffs are coming. Skydance’s co-CEOs have told staff to expect layoffs too. Studios have focused on cutting costs, but Hollywood needs to build for new formats, not just make old ones cheaper. Hollywood needs to fundamentally shift the way it operates, moving from producing finished products meant for passive consumption to developing stories and characters using input from their audiences. Instead of performing autopsies in hindsight, every major studio could put out drafts and iterate with audiences, the way creators do. Kane Parsons started Backrooms with one YouTube short and expanded it into a series when audiences responded positively. Vivienne Medrano released a fan-financed YouTube pilot of Hazbin Hotel ; A24 ordered a full series after it drew a huge following. Refining work using audience input doesn’t mean asking fans to vote on every creative choice. Strong directors have always filtered feedback, taking notes that tighten their narrative and discarding what dilutes their core vision. Borrowing a page from tech, studios could also be much more rigorous with data sourcing, A/B testing, and analysis to understand their audience’s behavior. This audience-centered approach can be applied to all parts of moviemaking. Films that perform well after an inexpensive tease, such as an animatic (storyboards that are cut together), can secure financing quickly, because financiers aren’t being asked to gamble many millions of dollars on an untested idea. Marketing happens in parallel with production. Your audience becomes not just fans but ambassadors, because they feel they are part of the process. The production becomes part of the story. Markiplier, a YouTuber whose real name is Mark Fischbach, created and financed a film, Iron Lung , which he planned to release in a small number of independent theaters. His fans emailed exhibitors until national chains picked it up. Vision is not replaced by data; instead, data can help studios find the audiences for visionary work, position it well, and understand which ambitious projects have real demand before committing hundreds of millions of dollars to them. If Orson Welles could have shared his early ideas with audiences in the 1940s, while making Citizen Kane , data wouldn’t have diluted the ambition of his deep-focus shots, broken timeline, and montages. Analyzing the public feedback could have helped him find his audience faster. Hollywood has a finite window to make these changes. Creators who already operate this way, such as MrBeast, are building their own production studios and will have less incentive to partner. Others will follow. [ Rose Horowitch: The film students who can no longer sit through films ] Studios are experimenting by launching short phone series on YouTube and TikTok, signing deals with top creators, and hiring creator-platform experts into executive positions. This is smart, but these initiatives still prioritize bringing existing franchises to new screens over developing stories alongside audiences. Dropping a digital executive into a traditional, risk-averse studio pipeline doesn’t change the entire studio’s culture. The business model, people, and creative culture that make a great film studio differ from those that are best for building a YouTube series or Roblox game. Hollywood doesn’t need to become a tech company, and Silicon Valley shouldn’t arrogantly assume that tech is superior to a story’s ability to move culture. Legacy studios still have what many creators need: capital, global marketing, distribution know-how, and deep story expertise. Just as Disney secured its future by partnering with and acquiring Pixar, today’s legacy studios need to collaborate with a new class of studios, ones that know how to build on creator platforms, are rooted in Hollywood storytelling, and treat technologists and artists equally. The Disney-Pixar relationship worked because Bob Iger gave Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull real power over Disney Animation. Other Hollywood acquisitions of gaming studios or creator talent have struggled when the acquired company lacked similar authority. A real partnership would allow legacy media to originate ideas on new platforms instead of being licensing arms for new players. AI will have its Toy Story moment. The studios that achieve it will know how to reach audiences on newer platforms, in formats that bring the audience along for the ride.

items.title: The False Comfort of Online Shopping
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. Between Black Friday deals, holiday gift guides, and the endless stream of targeted ads, it’s hard to avoid the temptation to buy something right now. And with just a few taps on our phones, we can purchase almost anything without having to leave the couch. Shopping has never been easier—or more solitary. In a new essay, Lily Meyer revisits Sophie Kinsella’s Confessions of a Shopaholic , 25 years after its publication in the United States, to explore how shopping has become an ever more isolating activity. The novel’s protagonist spends much of her time wandering through stores, accumulating debt. But at least her shopping takes place in the company of other people. Today, much of that experience has moved online, where influencers recommend products with the familiar tone of a friend, even as their relationships with followers remain fundamentally commercial. Meyer argues that modern shopping doesn't just isolate us from others; it can also create the illusion of companionship, blurring the line between genuine connection and consumption. Her essay offers a reminder that shopping can’t substitute for human connection. The Loneliness of Buying Too Many Things By Lily Meyer Confessions of a Shopaholic , 25 years later, suggests that the way we buy things has gotten too isolated. Read the article. Shopping Is Impossible By Rachel Sugar It’s never been more exhausting to buy stuff. Read the article. It’s Too Easy to Buy Stuff You Don’t Want By Amanda Mull Online shopping is too fast for good decisions. ( From 2023 ) Read the article. Still Curious? If you are still looking for something to delight the people in your life, explore the 2026 Atlantic gift guide , where The Atlantic ’s editorial team shares its gift recommendations for this holiday season. Black Friday nostalgia : If we’re going to worship consumerism and consumption, we should at least do it together, Annie Joy Williams wrote last year. Other Diversions Let’s not make reading a wellness trend. The real reason Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond A new milestone for life on Earth PS Courtesy of Jennie H. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. Last week, Jennie H. from Aitkin, Minnesota, shared a picture from January 1, 2024, of an ice bow over her farm, which “doesn’t happen often. It was well below zero that morning.” We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. — Rafaela

Comment la France perd les cerveaux étrangers : l’exemple de l’Algérien Noureddine Melikechi
items.description: Le climat de tension en France autour des étrangers et la montée de l’extrême droite font fuir les cerveaux étrangers. C'est le cas du physicien algérien de la NASA Noureddine Melikechi , qui raconte pourquoi il a quitté la France dans les années 1990 pour s'installer aux États-Unis. Les choses ont empiré aujourd'hui. C’est le moins que l'on puisse dire alors que l’extrême droite est aux portes du pouvoir. Noureddine Melikechi : « L’atmosphère en France ne me rassurait pas » « L’atmosphère en France ne me rassurait pas », raconte le savant dans l'ouvrage biographique « Noureddine Melikechi, un chemin de devoir et d’espoir », écrit par Rym Khelil. Tout récemment, l’université des Massachusetts a donné son nom à un de ses programmes de recherche. Cette distinction lui a valu les félicitations du président de la République Abdelmadjid Tebboune. Avant de devenir un pilier de la recherche en lasers et optique quantique au sein de la célèbre agence spatiale américaine, Melikechi était bien installé en France, après des études en Algérie et au Royaume-Uni. En 1994, raconte-t-il, il a réussi le concours de maître de conférences puis celui de professeur des universités une année plus tard. À l’été 1996, il rejoint l’université de Toulouse où, dit-il, il a beaucoup appris en travaillant avec une équipe de recherche toulousaine. « Le sujet était passionnant, les chercheurs très sympathiques, le matériel à l'avant-garde du progrès et la région toulousaine très belle, mais l'atmosphère en France ne me rassurait pas », confie-t-il. « Beaucoup de tensions demeuraient entre l'Algérie et la France » Noureddine Melikechi assure qu'il n'était pas le seul à sentir le climat pesant en France. Beaucoup de cerveaux étrangers, notamment algériens, songeaient déjà à partir. « L'environnement social dans lequel je projetais d'élever mes enfants me rebutait : beaucoup de tensions demeuraient entre l'Algérie et la France. Et plus je parlais à mes amis algériens travaillant dans les universités françaises, plus j'avais l'impression de nager à contre-courant. Eux tentaient de quitter la France pour rejoindre les États-Unis ! Beaucoup me confièrent leur sentiment de ne pas être traités comme les Français d'origine malgré leurs diplômes et leurs brillantes compétences professionnelles », dit-il. « Poussée de la propagande nationaliste et raciste » Le Doyen de Kennedy College of Sciences se rappelle particulièrement du cas d’un de ses amis d'enfance qui, à peine fini son doctorat en informatique, songeait sérieusement à quitter la France à cause de la montée de l’extrême droite dans les urnes. « Je me souviens d'une soirée chez lui, en 1995, où la discussion porta sur la campagne présidentielle française en cours. L'extrême droite, dirigée par Jean-Marie Le Pen, avait réalisé une percée notable. Cela me rebuta. La poussée de la propagande nationaliste et raciste, les affiches dans la rue, la banalisation de la haine de l'autre, tout cela nous fit remettre en question, ma femme et moi, nos projets d'installation en France. » « Finalement, notre environnement, nous le créons là où nous le souhaitons et nous pouvons être heureux un peu n'importe où. C'est bien ça le bonheur : la vie, le cœur et la raison. Cependant, lorsque l'environnement extérieur nous étouffe, comme c'est hélas le cas dans certaines sociétés contemporaines, le bonheur devient plus difficile à atteindre », explique Melikechi. Celui-ci n’a pas trop hésité avant de traverser l’Atlantique avec sa famille. À l'université du Delaware, il a eu « la chance », se félicite-t-il, de rencontrer des personnes « extrêmement intéressantes et inspirantes » qui ont profondément influencé sa carrière. « Là-bas, j'approfondis mes recherches dans la spectroscopie laser avec des applications dans la recherche médicale et spatiale », dit-il. La suite, c'est un énorme succès au sein de la plus prestigieuse agence spatiale au monde… L’article Comment la France perd les cerveaux étrangers : l’exemple de l’Algérien Noureddine Melikechi est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: AG directive: Amaliba calls for complaint unit to address misconduct
items.description: Director-General of the National Road Safety Authority (NRSA), Abraham Amaliba, has called on the Attorney General to establish a dedicated complaint unit to receive reports from citizens who experience misconduct from any of the investigative bodies. He said the unit would provide an accessible channel for ordinary Ghanaians to report officers accused of abusing their powers, including unlawful arrests, detention and other misconduct. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mr Amaliba argued that without a formal reporting mechanism, officers involved in such practices could continue to act with the belief that they would not be held accountable. “I think that there must be a complaint unit, so that any ordinary citizen who faces this challenge can go to the complaint unit and say police station B, Constable so and so, this is what he did,” he said. His comments follow the Attorney General’s recent statement outlining measures to address alleged abuses in the arrest, detention and prosecution of suspects, including unlawful detention, demands for payment during police bail and other forms of misconduct by law enforcement officers. Mr Amaliba described the statement on police misconduct as “revolutionary”, saying it was “the first time an Attorney General had catalogued the challenges confronting the system.” He, however, described the statement more as a reminder of existing legal obligations than a new directive, arguing that investigative bodies were already aware of the laws governing arrests, detention and the treatment of suspects. Mr Amaliba said the intervention was important in ensuring a balance between the rights of suspects and accused persons and the state’s responsibility to gather credible evidence for prosecution. He also raised concerns about the public perception that money must be paid to secure police bail. According to him, some citizens have become so accustomed to paying for bail that they struggle to accept explanations from lawyers that the process should not attract payment. He suggested that authorities review the language used in communicating bail conditions to make the process clearer to the public. Mr Amaliba further cautioned against blaming governments for police misconduct without evidence of direct political interference, arguing that the problem had persisted since the beginning of the Fourth Republic. “We need to ensure that we bring the fight to the doorstep of the state institutions that are doing those things,” he said.

items.title: Nigeria endorses Infantino for another term as FIFA president
items.description: Nigeria has declared its support for Gianni Infantino’s bid to retain the presidency of the world football governing body, FIFA, in the 2027 election. The Chairman of the National Sports Commission, Shehu Dikko, announced the Federal Government’s endorsement on Saturday during the 48th Ordinary General Assembly of the Confederation of African Football in Abuja. Speaking on behalf of President Bola Tinubu, Dikko said Nigeria would back Infantino’s re-election and called on other African football associations to support his continued leadership. “I must make it clear here on behalf of the Federal Government and in regard to the resolution of all the members of CAF that Nigeria firmly endorses Mr Gianni Infantino’s candidacy for the election. “This is a direct message that was given to us by the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Federal Republic of Nigeria,” he said. “We recognise Mr Gianni’s contribution to the advancement of football worldwide, particularly in Africa, and urge our fellow African member associations to stand firmly together in support of his continued leadership. “This is in our collective interest,” he added. The NSC chairman also praised Infantino’s administration, drawing on his experience in football management to argue that the FIFA president’s decisions had served the interests of the sport. “Before I conclude, if I put my heart as a football person, Mr President, as a former member of the NFL Exco, Chairman of the League, member of the FIFA Seconders Committee, and founding member of the World League Forum, I must tell you, Gianni’s decisions are very, very good for football. They are very apt for football,” he said. He maintained that Infantino’s central responsibility was to grow the game and generate more revenue, arguing that disagreements within football administration largely concerned how the funds were shared. “His main job is to develop football and bring revenues to football. He tries to do that. The entire issue we are seeing across the world here today has nothing to do with bringing the revenues or the distribution. It’s all about distributing these revenues,” Dikko said. Nigeria’s declaration came at the same gathering where CAF president Patrice Motsepe reiterated the continental body’s backing for Infantino’s re-election. Infantino, who became FIFA president in 2016, is seeking another four-year term at the election scheduled to hold in Morocco in March 2027 with French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo and Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima set to challenge him. The post Nigeria endorses Infantino for another term as FIFA president appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Le secrétaire général du MAE : « la Mauritanie est « affectée » par les dynamiques liées aux flux migratoires dans la région »
items.description: Le secrétaire général du ministère des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération africaine et des Mauritaniens de l’extérieur, l'ambassadeur Daman Hammer, a déclaré que « la Mauritanie, de par sa situation géographique au carrefour du Maghreb et de l’Afrique subsaharienne, et en tant qu’espace de communication et de circulation entre plusieurs régions, est directement concernée par les dynamiques liées aux flux migratoires transatlantiques en Afrique de l’Ouest ». Il s’exprimait lors de sa participation aux travaux de la conférence ministérielle consacrée au lancement du processus régional de coopération en matière de migration en Afrique de l’Ouest, qui s’est tenue à Dakar, du 18 au 20 novembre dernier, en présence de représentants de quinze pays africains. Le diplomate mauritanien a souligné que « la réponse à ces défis exige une responsabilité partagée et une coopération étroite entre les pays d’origine, de transit, de destination et de retour ». Il a évoqué « les priorités de la Mauritanie en matière de gouvernance des mouvements migratoires et de coopération régionale, qui comprennent la préservation de la souveraineté nationale, le renforcement de la coopération frontalière, la garantie du contrôle national des données relatives à l’immigration, la facilitation des mouvements migratoires organisés, la modernisation des postes-frontières, ainsi que le renforcement de la lutte contre la falsification de documents et les réseaux de trafic de migrants ». Il s’est également félicité « du lancement d’un processus régional de coopération durable, mené par les États et dont les priorités sont définies en fonction de leurs choix souverains et de leurs besoins nationaux ».

items.description: The Minister for Roads and Highways, Governs Kwame Agbodza, has indicated that it was an honour for him to be inducted as a Fellow of the Ghana Institute of Architects (GIA). He expressed his appreciation for being conferred with the highest fellowship distinction in his profession. “The highest honour your profession can give you is inducting you into the hall of fellows of your profession”, he said. He emphasised his commitment to promoting the architecture profession’s agenda, which currently focuses on advocating for a legislative instrument and policies to support an initiative to preserve the country’s architectural heritage. Mr Agbodza said that “I feel very honoured and also challenged to make sure that I carry the fact of colleagues in government in whatever I do as a public officer”. The short induction ceremony was held during the Institute’s 2026 Annual General Meeting (AGM) in Ho, the Volta Regional capital. The fellowship, the highest distinction awarded by the professional body, was conferred on him in recognition of his contributions to the profession, governance and the country’s development. Mr Agbodza, a Chartered Architect registered in both the United Kingdom and Ghana, has served as the Member of Parliament for Adaklu in the Volta Region since 2013 and as Minister for Roads and Highways. He has also served as Minority Chief Whip, a member of the Environment, Science and Technology Committee, and Vice-Chairman of the Roads and Transport Committee. He is a member of the Royal Institute of British Architects, the Ghana Institute of Architects, the UK Architects Registration Board and the Architects Registration Council of Ghana. Mr Agbodza holds a Bachelor of Science (BSc) in Architecture from the University of Science and Technology, Kumasi; a postgraduate Diploma in Architecture from the University of East London; and a professional practice qualification from the University of Westminster. He is a Chartered Architect and has led several healthcare, educational and residential development projects in Ghana and the United Kingdom. He also served as Principal Consultant at Kay + Partners Ltd, where he managed projects in both countries.

items.title: Tunisie | Nouvelle taxonomie climatique pour orienter les investissements verts
items.description: La Tunisie se dote d’une taxonomie climatique nationale, un nouvel outil de référence destiné à orienter les investissements publics et privés vers la transition écologique, la réduction des émissions de gaz à effet de serre et l’adaptation au changement climatique. Et identifie 100 activités économiques qui participent à l’atténuation du changement climatique. Ce document, publié par le Programme des Nations Unies pour le développement (Pnud), a été élaboré par le ministère de l’Environnement en collaboration avec le Conseil bancaire et financier (CBF), avec le soutien de l’initiative «Climate Promise» et du Fonds pour l’environnement mondial (FEM). Le nouveau système de classification identifie, en matière d’atténuation du changement climatique, 100 activités économiques réparties en trois catégories : 25 activités «habilitantes» , 22 activités à faible émission de carbone et 53 activités de transition. Une attention particulière est accordée au secteur agricole, stratégique pour la sécurité alimentaire du pays et particulièrement exposé aux effets de la sécheresse. Parmi les activités identifiées figurent l’agriculture biologique et de conservation, la culture des légumineuses, la restauration des terres dégradées, l’agroforesterie et la gestion durable des forêts. En ce qui concerne l’adaptation au changement climatique, le document prévoit également le développement de cultures résistantes à la sécheresse et aux températures élevées, l’irrigation au goutte-à-goutte et de précision, la restauration des zones humides ainsi que la gestion intégrée des bassins versants. Les secteurs de la pêche et de l’aquaculture sont également concernés, notamment à travers des mesures de protection des infrastructures portuaires face à l’élévation du niveau de la mer, le développement d’installations d'élevage piscicole en circuit fermé et la recherche d’espèces plus résilientes à la hausse des températures marines. La taxonomie englobe également les énergies renouvelables, l’efficacité énergétique, la mobilité électrique, le transport ferroviaire, le recyclage des déchets ainsi que la décarbonation progressive des industries manufacturières et agroalimentaires. L’objectif est de fournir aux banques, aux entreprises, aux investisseurs internationaux et aux institutions publiques des critères communs pour l’évaluation environnementale des projets, favorisant ainsi la mobilisation de capitaux vers des activités compatibles avec les priorités climatiques nationales et renforçant la transparence de la finance durable. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans le cadre des engagements pris par la Tunisie au titre de l’Accord de Paris, notamment l’objectif — fixé dans la contribution nationale actualisée en 2021 — de réduire de 45 % l’intensité carbone de l’économie d’ici 2030, par rapport aux niveaux de 2010. I. B. L’article Tunisie | Nouvelle taxonomie climatique pour orienter les investissements verts est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Pont de Crimée : Zelensky renouvelle ses menaces de destruction
items.description: « Ce pont ne restera pas en place. » La menace de Volodymyr Zelensky est sans equivoque. Interroge par NBC News le 20 novembre, le dirigeant ukrainien a renouvele sa menace contre le pont de Crimee, quelques jours apres les attaques des 16 et 17 novembre qui ont interrompu la circulation sur l'ouvrage. Pour justifier sa position, il invoque les attaques russes contre des ponts ukrainiens : « C'est pourquoi nous repondrons a ses attaques contre nos ponts. » Il presente ainsi la liaison entre la peninsule et le territoire russe comme une cible legitime. Long de 19 kilometres, le pont comprend une route et une voie ferree empruntees par des civils. Riposte de Moscou Le 19 novembre, lors de sa conference de presse en marge du forum de l'APEC a Shenzhen, Vladimir Poutine a souligne le caractere civil du pont : « Tout d'abord, je tiens a dire que le pont de Crimee est un ouvrage exclusivement civil. Depuis tres longtemps deja — d'ailleurs, j'en avais donne la consigne directe — nous n'utilisons plus le pont de Crimee pour transporter du materiel militaire, ni pour y deplacer des munitions. Nous n'avons meme pas fait transiter de petrole ni de produits petroliers par le pont. Il s'agit d'un ouvrage exclusivement civil. » Les consequences depassent les reparations materielles. Vladimir Poutine avait envisage avec le Conseil de securite russe un accord limitant les frappes contre les infrastructures energetiques et en mer Noire. Apres les attaques contre le pont, Moscou a ecarte cette possibilite. Le chef de l'etat a prevenu : « Mais apres les frappes contre le pont de Crimee, nous n'allons pas negocier. Nous allons riposter. Et j'aimerais que tout le monde le sache. J'estime que nos ripostes, comme je viens de le dire, seront beaucoup plus dures que les actes commis par le regime de Kiev contre ce pont. » Des frappes ukrainiennes contre le pont Dans la nuit du 15 au 16 novembre, une premiere attaque ukrainienne a entraîne une longue interruption du trafic routier. Une nouvelle frappe, dans la nuit du 16 au 17 novembre, a ensuite endommage une portion de chaussee ainsi que la structure de l'ouvrage. La circulation des trains a ete interrompue a son tour. Les autorites ont lance les reparations et organise des itineraires alternatifs. Le Comite d'enquete russe a ouvert une procedure pour acte terroriste. Aucune victime n'avait ete signalee au lendemain des deux premieres attaques. Une troisieme frappe, le 19 novembre, a entraîne une nouvelle suspension temporaire du trafic ferroviaire.

items.title: Kofi Tonto backs purchase of presidential jet but says Ghana should have acquired a bigger aircraft
items.description: A National Communications Member of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Kofi Tonto, has defended the government’s decision to acquire a new presidential aircraft, arguing that the President deserves adequate security, comfort and protection to perform his official duties. However, he believes Ghana should have purchased a bigger aircraft to serve the country’s presidential travel needs. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mr Tonto said he had no objection to the state investing in a presidential jet, provided adequate measures were in place to ensure that the President delivered on his responsibilities. His comments follow the government’s acquisition of a US$60.68 million Dassault Falcon 6X presidential aircraft, which arrived in Ghana on November 16. The aircraft is intended to replace the ageing Falcon 900EX, which the government says has experienced recurring technical problems, including fuel leaks, corrosion and engine-related faults. Mr Tonto argued that the acquisition of a dedicated presidential aircraft should not be considered unnecessary, given the importance of ensuring the safety, security and convenience of the country’s leader during official travels. He compared the decision to purchasing personal vehicles, noting that individuals invest in durable, safe and comfortable cars to improve their mobility and productivity despite having other financial responsibilities. He said Ghana, as a nation approaching 70 years of independence, could reasonably invest in an aircraft to support the President’s official functions. “I believe we should have purchased a bigger aircraft. I believe a President deserves the protection, the security, the safety and also the convenience to perform his duties. So, I have absolutely no issues if, as a nation state, we decide to procure an aircraft for the President to perform his functions,” he said. Mr Tonto, however, stressed that the benefits associated with the presidential aircraft must be matched by the President’s performance and commitment to national development. He said the country did not necessarily have to resolve all its challenges before making investments that could improve the efficiency of the presidency. “If a nation like Ghana, 70 years, and we decide to buy a presidential jet for our President, I think it is okay, if we can put in place the mechanisms to ensure that the President who is enjoying these benefits is performing to the optimal level required for this nation to move forward,” he added. Three options for presidential travel Mr Tonto also identified three possible arrangements available to the country for presidential international travel: using commercial flights, hiring private aircraft or owning a dedicated presidential jet. He said the decision to acquire an aircraft could be justified by the need to maintain the dignity and status of Ghana as a sovereign state during official presidential engagements. He noted that owning a presidential aircraft would give the country greater control over the President’s travel arrangements while providing the security and convenience required for official assignments. Reflecting on the history of presidential air travel, Mr Tonto cited an incident involving former President Nana Akufo-Addo, whose aircraft reportedly encountered engine-related problems while returning to Ghana from the United States. He said the incident, which occurred before 2018, contributed to discussions about the need for Ghana to acquire a new presidential aircraft. According to him, the former President had previously relied on commercial or hired aircraft for international travel before the incident heightened concerns about the country’s presidential air transport arrangements. Mr Tonto maintained that while the government could have opted to continue hiring private aircraft or using commercial flights, acquiring a presidential jet was a legitimate option. He nevertheless reiterated that he would have preferred a larger aircraft, suggesting that the country’s investment should adequately meet the needs of the presidency.

items.title: États-Unis : la GMD-USA apporte son soutien à la candidature de Mohamed Sy au Sénat
items.description: La candidature de Mohamed Sy, président du Conseil des Guinéens de l’étranger (CGE), au Sénat continue d’enregistrer des soutiens au sein de la diaspora guinéenne. Aux États-Unis, la coordination générale de la GMD-USA vient officiellement d’afficher son appui au candidat. Dans une lettre ouverte adressée aux Guinéens vivant aux États-Unis, dont Guineefutur.info détient copie, Mouctar Camara, coordinateur général de la GMD-USA, a fait connaître la position de son organisation en faveur de Mohamed Sy. Dans le document, l’organisation présente cette démarche comme une contribution au débat sur la représentation des Guinéens de l’étranger au sein des institutions nationales. La GMD-USA met notamment en avant le parcours de Mohamed Sy à la tête du Conseil des Guinéens de l’étranger, ainsi que les valeurs de dialogue, de rassemblement, de responsabilité et de défense de l’intérêt général. Elle annonce par ailleurs son intention de mobiliser ses plateformes de communication, notamment Facebook, Instagram et TikTok, pour faire connaître sa position, le parcours du candidat et ses propositions. Par cette prise de position publique, Mouctar Camara et son organisation entendent ainsi apporter leur soutien à la candidature de Mohamed Sy au Sénat. items.title: Sonacos : la Chine prête à absorber toute la production de la prochaine campagne
items.description: La Sonacos renforce son offensive sur le marché chinois. Au terme d’une mission en Chine, du 7 au 14 novembre, son Directeur général, Cheikh Ahmeth Tidiane Gueye, a noué des partenariats commerciaux visant à écouler la totalité de la production d’huile d’arachide et de graines décortiquées de la prochaine campagne. Une avancée qui intervient en parallèle d’un programme de modernisation de l’outil industriel. La Chine pourrait devenir un débouché majeur pour la prochaine campagne arachidière de la SONACOS. En déplacement dans l’Empire du Milieu du 7 au 14 novembre 2026, le Directeur général, Cheikh Ahmeth Tidiane Gueye, accompagné de ses collaborateurs, a conclu des partenariats stratégiques avec plusieurs acteurs de l’industrie agroalimentaire chinoise, avec en ligne de mire l’achat de la totalité de la production d’huile d’arachide et de graines d’arachide décortiquées de l’entreprise, indique un communiqué. Cette perspective marque un tournant dans la stratégie commerciale de la Société nationale de commercialisation des oléagineux du Sénégal. La sécurisation de débouchés à l’international constitue un enjeu majeur pour écouler les volumes produits, renforcer les recettes commerciales et améliorer la valorisation de l’arachide sénégalaise. En ciblant le marché chinois, la SONACOS cherche ainsi à consolider ses positions à l’export et à inscrire ses produits dans des circuits commerciaux à fort potentiel. Un débouché stratégique pour la filière Au-delà des engagements commerciaux, cette démarche pourrait contribuer à donner davantage de visibilité à la campagne arachidière, en offrant des perspectives d’écoulement pour les produits transformés par l’entreprise. Elle pose également la question de la capacité de la SONACOS à mieux capter la valeur ajoutée de la production nationale, à travers la transformation industrielle et l’accès à de nouveaux marchés. A lire aussi : Commercialisation agricole : 105 milliards de FCFA mobilisés, 44 milliards d’arriérés à régler La mission a également été consacrée au suivi des investissements industriels. Le Directeur général et sa délégation ont visité les partenaires chargés de fabriquer les nouveaux équipements destinés aux unités de production de la SONACOS. L’objectif est de s’assurer de l’avancement des projets de modernisation et de la concrétisation des investissements engagés pour améliorer les performances de l’appareil productif. La coopération avec les partenaires chinois ne se limite pas aux échanges commerciaux. Les discussions ont également porté sur les perspectives de transfert de technologie dans le domaine de la transformation agroalimentaire (food processing). Cette orientation ouvre des perspectives en matière de renforcement des compétences, de diversification de l’offre et de développement de nouveaux produits issus des ressources agricoles locales. Oumar FEDIOR

items.title: ‘A fine gift to our generation’, Olajengbesi hails Davido on birthday
items.description: Human rights lawyer, Pelumi Olajengbesi, has described Afrobeats star David Adeleke, popularly known as Davido, as one of the fine gifts to the present generation. In a Facebook post on Saturday to celebrate the singer’s birthday, Olajengbesi, who was the campaign spokesman for the re-election of Davido’s uncle, Governor Ademola Adeleke of Osun State, applauded the greatness of the Adeleke family. Olajengbesi said, “Happy Birthday Davido, thank you for who you are to everyone who meets you. You are one of the finest gifts to our generation. I am not just grateful to you and your family, I am indebted for life. “I have seen men, I have seen great families, but I have not seen many like the Adelekes. Blessed by God, graced by men, strengthened by love, bound together by service, and united by a generosity of spirit that transcends generations. “There is something extraordinary about a family whose greatness is measured not merely by wealth, influence or accomplishments, but by the number of lives they have touched, the doors they have opened and the hope they continue to inspire in others. “I pray that the Almighty God continues to preserve you, enlarge your coast, strengthen your home and grant you greater accomplishments. May your light never grow dim, and may generations yet unborn find inspiration in the legacy you are building.” Back in September, Davido endorsed the ambition of Olajengbesi to contest the Oriade-Obokun Federal Constituency seat in the 2027 general elections. Davido had described Olajengbesi as his next project following the governor’s victory at the poll. Olajengbesi is contesting against Wole Oke of the All Progressives Congress, who has occupied the seat for 24 years. The lawyer has garnered support from the likes of popular singer Dapo Oyebanjo, aka D’banj; Spotlite Nation boss Moses Bliss; and Yoruba Nation campaigner Sunday Igboho, among others. items.title: CAF introduces U-17 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations
items.description: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has approved the establishment of an Under-17 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations. The decision was reached on Saturday during a meeting of the CAF Executive Committee in Abuja, Nigeria, under the leadership of the body’s president, Patrice Motsepe. CAF announced the development in a statement published on its official website. “The new competition will provide more opportunities for young African female footballers to compete at international level, gain valuable experience and develop their talents,” CAF said. “This decision reflects CAF’s commitment to strengthening women’s football, particularly at youth level, and creating a stronger pathway for the next generation of African footballers.” Following the approval, CAF also invited member associations interested in hosting the maiden edition to begin submitting their bids. In a separate decision, the Executive Committee approved the commencement of the bidding process for the 2028 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations. Interested member associations have three weeks to forward their hosting proposals to the CAF Secretariat. The 2028 edition of the tournament is scheduled for March and April, while its qualifying campaign is expected to commence in April 2027. The meeting also considered plans to strengthen refereeing across African football, with Motsepe stressing the importance of increased investment in the training, development and performance of match officials. CAF Referees Committee chairman, Olivier Safari Kabene, presented several proposals, including the CAF Elite Referees Project, which is scheduled to hold its first training programme in the final week of November 2026. The body also plans to introduce its Next Generation Referees programme to prepare emerging officials for future assignments. CAF added that it was developing a referees’ manual to provide uniform guidelines and improve consistency in officiating across its competitions. items.title: Héritage des JOJ : le Premier ministre plaide pour « Le Soleil » et l’Aps
items.description: Lors de la réunion d’évaluation des JOJ « Dakar 2026 », tenue vendredi au Building administratif, le Premier ministre, Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed Lô, a salué le travail accompli par les médias publics, notamment la RTS, « Le Soleil » et l’Aps. Après avoir évoqué les moyens importants mobilisés au profit de la télévision nationale, le chef du gouvernement a plaidé pour que les deux autres médias publics puissent aussi, eux aussi, bénéficier de ces Jeux, notamment sur les plans financier et matériel. Vendredi, au cours de la réunion des JOJ « Dakar 2026 », le Premier ministre a rappelé qu’outre la RTS, les autres médias publics avaient également pris une part active à la couverture des JOJ. Il a ainsi plaidé pour une prise en compte de leurs efforts dans la répartition des retombées de cet événement. « Nous nous sommes occupés de la RTS, mais “Le Soleil” et l’Aps ont également réalisé un excellent travail », a affirmé Ahmadou Alhaminou Mohamed Lô. Et de poursuivre : « Si l’on entend que la RTS a reçu des milliards, il ne faut pas oublier que “Le Soleil” et l’Aps étaient eux aussi sur le terrain et qu’ils continuent d’y être jusqu’à présent. Je pense qu’il est pertinent de nous pencher sur leur situation financière et matérielle. Cela fait également partie de l’héritage. » Un plaidoyer qui ouvre ainsi la perspective d’une meilleure prise en compte des besoins des deux autres médias publics dans le dispositif de valorisation des acquis des JOJ « Dakar 2026 ». Prenant la parole lors de cette rencontre, le directeur général de la RTS, Pape Alé Niang, est revenu sur les efforts consentis par ses équipes pour assurer la couverture audiovisuelle de cet événement. Il a, à ce propos, salué l’accompagnement de l’État et la collaboration avec le Comité international olympique (CIO) et Olympic Broadcasting Services (Obs), le prestataire chargé de la production audiovisuelle des Jeux. « Je pense qu’en termes d’héritage, comme vous l’avez évoqué, Monsieur le Premier ministre, vous avez totalement libéré les moyens financiers nécessaires », a-t-il reconnu. Avant de souligner l’ampleur de la mission confiée à la télévision nationale : « Le plus gros du travail a été confié à la RTS, sous la supervision, bien entendu, d’Obs. Nous avons particulièrement travaillé avec le CIO et Obs et, au terme de ce travail, le résultat est fortement apprécié par tout le monde. » A. DEMBÉLÉ

items.title: Quand l’État reprend sa place à Siguiri, ça dérange qui ? (Par Bernard Leno)
items.description: À mon avis, l'interdiction de l'orpaillage clandestin n'est pas une punition contre qui que ce soit, c'est un acte de souveraineté. On le sait, pendant trop longtemps, cette partie du nord-est de la Guinée a vécu dans la pagaille. Des sites anarchiques, des rivières empoisonnées au mercure, des forêts rasées, des jeunes livrés à eux-mêmes, et surtout des ressources pillées sous nos yeux. En décidant d'y mettre fin, les autorités de Conakry prennent leurs responsabilités: protéger les ressources du pays, qui appartiennent à tout le peuple, et protéger la vie des populations. Car, sans eau propre, sans terres cultivables, il n'y a sans aucun doute pas d'avenir pour la Haute Guinée. Loin d’être une guerre contre les orpailleurs ou contre une quelconque catégorie de ressortissants étrangers, cette décision est une invitation à l'ordre et à un orpaillage digne et encadré. Et c'est là que le comportement de certains « activistes » ouest-africains est déplorable sur TikTok et Facebook. Ne digèrent-ils pas que la Guinée prenne ses responsabilités ? Quand ce secteur était dans le désordre à Siguiri, ils se moquaient. Maintenant que la Guinée met de l'ordre, ils crient. En fait, ce n'est pas l'orpaillage qui les dérange, c'est de voir la Guinée debout. Qu'ils se calment. La Guinée n'a pas besoin de leur permission pour protéger Siguiri. La souveraineté, ça ne se négocie pas en live TikTok ou Facebook. Revenez encore ! La prochaine fois, on ne vous loupera pas ! Bernard Leno L’article Quand l'État reprend sa place à Siguiri, ça dérange qui ? (Par Bernard Leno) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: La ministre de la santé a confirmé que 18 des centres de santé ouverts récemment à Nouakchott sont désormais opérationnels
items.description: La ministre de la Santé, Naha Hamdi Mouknass, a déclaré que 18 centres de santé sur les 28 nouveaux centres de Nouakchott sont désormais opérationnels, dans le cadre du programme d'urgence pour le développement de la ville. La ministre a ajouté, dans un discours prononcé vendredi soir à Nouakchott lors de l’ouverture du XIXe Congrès national de pédiatrie, que la santé maternelle et infantile occupe une place centrale dans le programme du président Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani, « qui vise à permettre aux citoyens d’accéder à des services de santé plus proches et de meilleure qualité ». Elle a souligné que le gouvernement s’efforce de concrétiser cette orientation en élargissant l’offre de soins, en renforçant les ressources humaines et en améliorant la préparation des établissements de santé, précisant que ces efforts englobent le suivi de la grossesse et de l’accouchement, les soins aux nouveau-nés, ainsi que la mise à disposition de vaccins, de services de nutrition et de traitements. Il y a environ un mois, le président mauritanien Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani avait chargé le gouvernement d’accélérer la mise en service de 28 centres de santé à Nouakchott, en veillant à ce que le personnel médical, les équipements et les fournitures nécessaires soient en place, et en garantissant leur capacité à fournir des services de santé.

KGL Foundation commissions GH¢5m ICT and STEM centre at Aburi Girls
items.description: The KGL Foundation has commissioned a GH¢5 million ICT and STEM Centre at Aburi Girls Senior High School to strengthen students’ access to science and technology education. The commissioning of Phase One of the Caroline Agyemang Dadey ICT and STEM Centre took place on November 20, 2026, as part of the school’s 80th anniversary celebrations. Designed by the school’s 2001 Year Group, the facility is intended to provide students with opportunities for practical learning, digital skills development and innovation in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). The centre is named after Caroline Agyemang Dadey, Director of the KGL Foundation and a member of the KGL Group of Companies. She is also an alumna of Aburi Girls, having been a member of the Class of 1978. Addressing the ceremony, Mrs Dadey called for greater national attention to girls’ education and increased private-sector involvement in addressing gaps in the education system. “The world we live in today is technologically driven, and it is important for alumni to support schools in various ways. ICT is a crucial area to invest in, as it allows our girls to compete globally,” she said. The centre features laboratories, digital learning resources and collaborative spaces intended to support hands-on learning and encourage students to explore STEM disciplines. The commissioning brought together alumni, educators, students and other stakeholders as the school marked eight decades of its contribution to girls’ education. The Aburi Girls project forms part of the KGL Group’s wider community development and institutional support initiatives. Two weeks before the commissioning, the KGL Foundation commissioned the Dr Alex Dadey Alumni Centre at the University of Ghana. This was followed by the unveiling of the Alex A. Dadey Sports Centre at Mfantsipim School in Cape Coast. Reflecting on the three projects, Mrs Dadey said: “Three institutions, three landmark projects, one enduring family philosophy: to give back to the institutions that helped shape who we are.” The school’s 80th anniversary celebrations also include workshops, guest lectures and community outreach programmes aimed at encouraging students to consider careers in STEM fields.

items.title: Des récifs artificiels aux îles Kerkennah pour protéger la pêche
items.description: Restaurer les écosystèmes marins, favoriser la reconstitution des stocks halieutiques et préserver les activités de pêche traditionnelle grâce à l’installation de récifs artificiels. Tels sont les objectifs d’un projet pilote financé par le Fonds pour l’environnement mondial (FEM) et impliquant les pêcheurs artisanaux, qui a été présenté, le 19 novembre 2026, dans l’archipel tunisien des Kerkennah, au large de Sfax. Ce projet vise également à renforcer la gestion participative de la future aire marine et côtière protégée des îlots septentrionaux de l’archipel. L’initiative, dont la mise en œuvre est prévue jusqu’en mars 2027, s’inscrit dans le cadre du programme méditerranéen FishEBM Med, dédié à la gestion de la pêche fondée sur les écosystèmes et au développement de l’économie bleue. Le projet bénéficie de la coordination technique du Centre d’activités régionales pour les aires spécialement protégées (CAR/ASP), dans le cadre du Programme des Nations Unies pour l’environnement (Pnue). Sa mise en œuvre est confiée à deux associations locales : Kantara Save Earth et l’Association de Kraten pour le développement durable, la culture et les loisirs (AKDDCL). Le premier axe d’intervention prévoit des études préliminaires, ainsi que la réalisation et l’immersion, sur les fonds marins, de structures artificielles destinées à créer des habitats favorables à la faune marine et à la biodiversité. Le second axe porte sur le suivi scientifique des effets de ces structures sur les écosystèmes, la création d’un espace itinérant d’éducation à l’environnement et l’aménagement d’un sentier sous-marin à vocation pédagogique et naturaliste. Une attention particulière sera accordée à l’implication des pêcheurs artisanaux, par le biais de consultations et d’ateliers participatifs, en valorisant leur connaissance des fonds marins et des dynamiques marines locales, notamment dans le cadre de la lutte contre la pêche illégale. Les îles Kerkennah constituent l’un des principaux conservatoires des traditions de pêche en Méditerranée. On y trouve notamment la «charfia» , une technique ancestrale de pêche passive qui utilise des structures fixes constituées de palmes, tirant parti des courants et des marées ; cette pratique a été inscrite en 2020 par l’Unesco sur la liste du patrimoine culturel immatériel de l’humanité. L’objectif est de faire de l’archipel un laboratoire de gestion durable des ressources marines, en conciliant la préservation de la biodiversité et la sauvegarde des activités économiques des communautés côtières, selon un modèle potentiellement reproductible dans d’autres zones de la Méditerranée. I. B. L’article Des récifs artificiels aux îles Kerkennah pour protéger la pêche est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Fighting a Radical Militia Was Not Part of the Plan
items.description: In late October, I met a Yemeni military officer at a high-end mall in Riyadh. He wore a dishdasha and had the gruff, weary manner of an aging career soldier. His unit had been fighting the Houthi militia in southern Yemen, more than 800 miles from the immaculate, marble-floored refuge at the center of the Saudi capital where we ordered coffee. He was mapping the battlefield on the table with his hands, describing how the latest round of fighting had played out, when cellphones began beeping simultaneously all around us: an incoming-missile warning. Moments later, loud booms echoed through the mall, followed by audible gasps from nearby tables and a child’s cry of fear. Shoppers froze in their tracks, some glancing anxiously toward the glass dome above us. The Yemeni officer looked at me without speaking. A grim smile played on his lips, as if to say: They are all learning about the Houthis now. The missiles were intercepted, but the moment stayed with me. A new reality was intruding on a population coddled for years by visions of a frictionless post-oil future, when new technologies would keep everyone happy and entertained. Saudi Arabia is at war. The Houthis have demonstrated, by means of recurring missile barrages, that they can shut down much of the country’s economy at will. A deadly strike on the main airport in Riyadh killed at least 14 people in mid-October and injured hundreds. More than a month later, few flights have resumed. “The kingdom today faces the most dangerous crisis in its history, the Saudi journalist Abdulrahman al-Rashed told a Saudi podcaster last month. That kind of candor is extremely hard to come by in Saudi Arabia. None of the Saudi or Yemeni officials I met in Riyadh in October would speak with me on the record. They told me that the monarchy is now taking the Houthi threat far more seriously than in the past. Riyadh has struck deals to bring thousands of soldiers from Pakistan and Syria to help defend the country’s border with Yemen. But these efforts may not be enough. The Houthis are building up their forces too, with help from Iran, China, North Korea, and Russia. [ Graeme Wood: The only thing the Houthis have done successfully ] The Houthis are no longer the rebel upstarts of a decade ago. They are well on their way to becoming the North Korea of the Arab world: an insular, well-armed, and fanatical statelet that poses a threat to the entire region. They have an AI-assisted weapons industry and have studied the Ukraine war; their information operations are way ahead of their Saudi and Yemeni rivals’. The Houthis could soon become more dangerous than Iran, their long-standing patron. The Saudi military was not designed for this kind of war. The country’s rulers have long been reluctant to build an army that could one day pose a threat to the monarchy. Even now they have dismissed the notion of sending their own troops, apart from elite special forces already deployed in Yemen, to fight the Houthis. But they may soon find that you cannot rely on foreigners when your country is facing a very real threat of invasion. The current Houthi military offensive began in September, when the group captured the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia’s leaders believe that this plan was largely devised by Iran. In October, I met with a senior Saudi official who described a strategy coordinated by Tehran and its allies in the “Axis of Resistance” over the past several months. The latest chapter, the official said, began in the spring, when President Trump ordered the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. That left Tehran with limited options to retaliate, so Iranian officials met with their Houthi allies and persuaded them to launch an offensive on the Bab el-Mandeb. The Iranians, the official said, agreed to help make it happen. A Houthi delegation attended the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran in July, he told me, and when it returned, the Mahan Air flight that carried it also conveyed a whole team of Axis military technicians and commanders, including two North Koreans, a Syrian who had been part of the Assad regime, and members of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and of Lebanese Hezbollah, the Shiite militia. The plane was loaded with cash and weapons, including drone parts and missile-guidance systems, the Saudi official told me. (Some details of the Mahan Air flight have been reported previously, including the weapons and Iranian officers on board.) The Saudis had gotten word of the plane’s cargo and bombed the runway of the airport in the Yemeni capital to prevent it from landing. But the flight was diverted to Hodeida, a city on the Red Sea coast that is also under Houthi control, and landed there. Separately, the Saudi official told me, Russia delivered a large shipment of weapons and technology, concealed under thousands of tons of wheat. If the Saudi official’s account is accurate, it would suggest that the Houthis are receiving more international support than ever. Even if the report was exaggerated for the benefit of an American journalist—Saudi officials are desperate to get more military assistance from the United States—it still points to a larger truth about what the Houthis have become. The Houthis are the world’s problem. They have proved that they can block a waterway that carries about 15 percent of the world’s trade. They now control about a third of Yemen’s territory and most of its population, and aim to conquer it all. Their use of child soldiers has been well documented for a decade, as has their frequent use of torture, arbitrary detentions, and disappearances. Their rule is rooted in a revolutionary ideology that does not stop at Yemen’s borders and that thrives on constant war. They have challenged Saudi control of Mecca and Medina, Islam’s holiest cities, and they often boast that they will liberate Jerusalem. [ Thomas Wright: The price of defeat in Iran ] These are not empty ambitions. The Houthis are constantly expanding their missile and drone production, using fiber optics and other materials supplied by China. Evidence recently came to light that they have used the AI tool Claude to improve their guided-missile technology. They have developed pragmatic relationships with al-Qaeda and the al-Shabaab terrorist group, despite sectarian differences (the Houthis adhere to an offshoot of Shiite Islam; the other two groups are Sunni). And, in a show of political dexterity and ideological fervor, they have been recruiting and providing training to ethnic and tribal subgroups throughout the Horn of Africa, in Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, and Sudan. These outreaches appear to be modeled on Iran’s efforts to build up regional allies, and could add more tinder to an already volatile region of Africa. For now, Saudi Arabia lies on the front line of any effort to contain the Houthis’ power. The United States is too deep in its war with Iran to provide anything more than minimal help, and the Europeans are focused on Ukraine. The other Gulf countries have good reasons to fight the Houthis, but for various reasons, they will not. The Omanis have been hedging their bets for years—allowing the Houthis to smuggle arms across their border with Yemen and providing some intelligence—in case the Houthis end up as the winners. The United Arab Emirates fought the Houthis inside Yemen for years alongside the Saudis, but late last year, long-running tensions between the two countries reached a breaking point, and the Saudis ordered the Emiratis to withdraw. The Emiratis’ absence has damaged the broader war effort. The Saudis, who have long backed the internationally recognized Yemeni government in Aden, organized a counteroffensive after the Houthis captured the Bab el-Mandeb. They embedded Saudi commandos with Yemeni government forces across the country. Some were killed in a devastating Houthi strike on October 19. The Saudi official I met in Riyadh told me that the near-term goal is to recapture all of the territory that was lost in September, and then secure some kind of truce. The Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have not yet achieved that, and it is not clear that they will. “I don’t see a way out unless the U.S. agrees to provide direct air support,” Nadwa al-Dawsari, an associate fellow at the Middle East Institute, told me. Even if the Saudis are able to achieve a respite from the fighting, the Houthis will retain the whip hand in the conflict, because they will still be able to strike the kingdom’s airports and oil facilities. And they will surely use any truce to continue expanding their military, as they have in the past. The Saudi official told me that the kingdom’s long-term plan is to build a larger and more unified Yemeni military that is capable of pushing the Houthis back and “eliminating their military capabilities.” That is a tall order. The Yemeni military officer I met in Riyadh last month described a fighting force that is hamstrung by clashing political and regional loyalties. “There are forces loyal to Islah”—the Yemeni Islamist party—“and they hate us,” he said, referring to his own more secular faction. (He did not need to add that the feeling is mutual.) In the south, many of the soldiers are more interested in creating a separate state than in fighting the Houthis. “The Houthis know all about the divisions on our side,” the officer said, “and they take advantage of it.” The Saudis bring problems of their own to the conflict. One is the kingdom’s culture of entitlement and corruption, which has bled into its behavior in Yemen. For decades, the Saudis maintained their influence in Yemen through a patronage system of stipends paid to tribal sheikhs and military figures, and they took a quasi-imperial view of Yemenis as primitive underlings. They had a reputation for paying their proxy soldiers so poorly or so late that some had to sell their weapons in order to feed their children. This pattern of behavior generated deep resentment, partly because the Yemenis got a glimpse of a different approach. The Emiratis spent decades fostering a culture of discipline and accountability in their own country, and in Yemen, they had a reputation for training their allies, paying them higher salaries, and demanding results in return. The Emiratis—who run a small but highly effective military of their own—therefore had far more success with their Yemeni recruits. The Saudis say they are reforming their system, but that will take time. The Saudis and their allies are now struggling to relieve the month-long Houthi siege of Taiz, one of Yemen’s largest cities. If the Houthis capture it, nothing but open roads will separate them from Aden, the base of Yemen’s internationally recognized government and its military headquarters. “There is nothing going on to defend Aden,” Henry Thompson, a Yemen expert who has worked with the United Nations, told me. (Just in the past few days, the threat to Aden has grown, and some signs of defensive preparations have become evident there.) The Houthis, meanwhile, have taken measures in the territories they control that could pull Yemeni troops into protracted conflict even if they succeed in retaking ground. Some recent seizures of cargo destined for Houthi ports have intercepted equipment for digging tunnels, including excavation tools and ventilation systems. The Houthis appear to have successfully imported large quantities of this kind of gear in recent years. [ Robert F. Worth: Saudi Arabia is running out of options ] “In Hodeida, the Houthis have built a city underneath the city,” Mohammed al-Basha, a Yemen analyst and the founder of the Basha Report, a geopolitical-risk advisory firm, told me. “For anyone trying to capture that place, it would be like going into Gaza.” For the moment, the war is not going well. After making some gains in October, the Saudi-backed forces announced on November 15 that they had been forced to withdraw from the area around the Bab el-Mandeb. I met several members of Yemen’s internationally recognized government in Riyadh—their rear base—and they tried to put on a brave face, with varying degrees of success. Some seem resigned to deeper losses. “The Houthis will take Aden, and they will keep going,” one told me. The current battlefield is in southern Yemen, but everyone I spoke with agreed that the Houthis will eventually open a new front in the north and attempt to invade Saudi Arabia. That would make it impossible for the Saudis to deny that they are at war. Until now, they have held firmly to the claim that this is an intra-Yemeni conflict, and that Saudi Arabia is a third party. But the Houthis have made clear for years that they consider themselves to be at war with Riyadh, and they frequently mock Yemen’s internationally recognized government as a Saudi fig leaf. Almost no one in Saudi Arabia wants to acknowledge the possibility that they could soon be forced to defend their country. “Why should we send our young men to defend the Bab el-Mandeb?” one official asked me in Riyadh. “The conflict is inside Yemen.” He went on to describe the Houthis as nothing more than an “annoyance.” None of the ordinary Saudis I spoke with in Riyadh, whether old friends or people I approached in cafés, seemed comfortable talking about the war. Saudi Arabia is an autocratic society where dissent can land a person in jail—but the reticence may also reflect the dissonance people feel between the war and everything their ruler has been telling them for the past decade. Saudi Arabia’s problems are supposed to be solved through technology and innovation. Being dragged into a bloody war with a radical militia is not part of that plan. It is not part of America’s plans, either—especially not since the Trump administration waged an expensive and largely futile air war against the Houthis lasting seven weeks in early 2025. But that could change. items.title: Saisie par la police mauritanienne de la plus importante quantité de drogue saisie à ce jour
items.description: La police mauritanienne a annoncé avoir démantelé un réseau de trafic de stupéfiants extrêmement dangereux, actif dans plusieurs pays voisins et qui prévoyait d'étendre ses activités à la Mauritanie. Dans un communiqué publié ce vendredi soir, elle a indiqué que le Bureau central de lutte contre les stupéfiants et les substances psychotropes avait réussi à mettre au jour ce réseau, après « trois mois d’enquête, grâce à des moyens et des techniques modernes de surveillance et de traçage ». Selon le communiqué de la police, le Bureau a mené « une opération de sécurité dans la région de « Decha », dans la wilaya du Hodh Chargui, à cinq kilomètres de la frontière orientale, qui a abouti à l’interception d’un véhicule de type « Toyota Hilux » utilisée par le réseau, à bord de laquelle se trouvaient deux personnes de nationalité étrangère, ainsi qu’une cargaison pesant une tonne et sept cents kilogrammes (1 700 kg) de cocaïne de haute qualité (crack) » D’après les déclarations des deux suspects, cette cargaison provenait d’un pays voisin et était destinée à un autre pays limitrophe, en passant par plusieurs zones adjacentes aux frontières est et nord-est du pays, selon le communiqué. Le communiqué a indiqué que « trois autres personnes de la même nationalité, directement liées à ce réseau, sont recherchées », soulignant que la quantité saisie lors de cette opération est « la plus importante de ce type parmi les opérations enregistrées à ce jour ».

items.title: Manhyia South MP urges AG to introduce legislative guidelines for granting bail
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Manhyia South, Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah, has urged the Attorney General to go beyond issuing directives on the protection of suspects’ rights and introduce clear legislative guidelines to regulate the exercise of discretionary powers in granting bail. He said the absence of clear guidelines for the administrative exercise of bail had created room for abuse of power, resulting in unnecessary hardship for individuals, business people and others caught up in the criminal justice system. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, the MP said the Attorney General should consider presenting a legislative instrument to Parliament to establish clear procedures for the exercise of bail powers. His comments follow the Attorney General’s directive requiring law enforcement and investigative agencies to comply with the constitutional 48-hour detention limit and other safeguards protecting arrested persons. The directive applies to institutions including the Ghana Police Service, the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), the National Intelligence Bureau (NIB) and the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC). It requires arrested persons to be informed of the reasons for their arrest and their right to legal representation, while prohibiting the use of arrest and detention to recover civil debts. It also demands respect for suspects’ right to silence and voluntary confessions and prohibits unlawful searches, torture and coercion. The agencies are further required to submit quarterly compliance reports to the Attorney-General detailing arrests, releases, court appearances and alleged violations of suspects’ rights. Mr Awuah acknowledged the importance of the directive but argued that further legal and institutional measures were needed to address the exercise of discretionary powers, particularly in relation to bail. Referring to Article 29 of the Constitution, he argued that the Attorney General should introduce specific guidelines or a legislative instrument to regulate the administrative exercise of bail powers. He said the issue extended beyond politicians, claiming that business people were also suffering from the actions of some law enforcement officials. “AG, for instance, must go beyond this. The Attorney General should go beyond this and bring a guideline or a legislative instrument to Parliament as to how the administrative exercise of power of bail may be exercised because we are inflicting pains,” he said. Mr Awuah further alleged that some business people were being targeted in ways that threatened Ghanaian businesses, warning that the abuse of institutional powers could have wider consequences for the economy. MP proposes parliamentary oversight The Manhyia South MP also outlined steps he intends to pursue through Parliament to strengthen oversight of the institutions affected by the Attorney-General’s directive. He said he could raise questions on the floor of Parliament and use his membership of the Legal Affairs Committee to push for closer scrutiny of the relevant institutions. He further proposed that the committee’s leadership consider organising visits to some of the agencies to assess their operations and verify the concrete measures being implemented to comply with the Attorney General’s instructions. According to him, parliamentary oversight should help establish whether the announced reforms are translating into practical changes within the institutions responsible for arrests, detention and bail administration. He, however, stressed that addressing the problem required cooperation among all stakeholders rather than isolated efforts. Mr Awuah called for a national commitment to ending the persistent abuse of power, insisting that Ghana must move beyond a situation where individuals suffer because of the discretionary authority exercised by public institutions. “I think that as a nation, we need to move beyond this constant abuse of power,” he added.
