items.title: Preterm birth: Understanding the risks, complications and care for babies born too soon
items.description: Every baby deserves a chance to survive and thrive. But for babies born too early, the journey to survival can be particularly challenging. As the world marks World Prematurity Month, MamaCare by Racheal is drawing attention to the health challenges associated with premature births and the need to support affected babies and their families. Premature birth, also known as preterm birth, occurs when a baby is born alive before completing 37 weeks of pregnancy. While a full-term pregnancy generally lasts about 40 weeks, babies born prematurely may not have had sufficient time for vital organs, including the lungs, brain, heart and digestive system, to develop fully. This leaves them vulnerable to complications that may require specialised medical attention and newborn care. Preterm births are classified according to gestational age into three main categories: Extremely preterm: Babies born before 28 weeks. Very preterm: Babies born between 28 and less than 32 weeks. Moderate to late preterm: Babies born between 32 to 36 weeks WHAT INCREASES THE RISK OF PRETERM BIRTH? Several maternal, medical and pregnancy-related factors can increase a woman’s risk of delivering prematurely. These include maternal conditions such as high blood pressure, pre-eclampsia, diabetes, kidney or heart disease and anaemia. Infections, including urinary tract infections, reproductive tract infections and malaria, may also increase the risk. Other pregnancy-related factors include multiple pregnancies, a previous history of preterm birth, cervical insufficiency, placental complications, vaginal bleeding and premature rupture of membranes. Lifestyle and social factors such as smoking, alcohol and harmful substance use, inadequate antenatal care, poor nutrition, severe stress and short intervals between pregnancies may also contribute. However, having one or more of these risk factors does not necessarily mean a woman will deliver prematurely. It highlights the importance of early assessment, regular antenatal care and appropriate medical attention. WARNING SIGNS OF PRETERM LABOUR EVERY PREGNANT WOMAN SHOULD KNOW These signs include: Regular abdominal tightening or contractions before 37 weeks of pregnancy. Persistent or unusual lower back pain, particularly when it comes and goes. Menstrual-like cramps. Changes in vaginal discharge. Vaginal bleeding or spotting. A sudden gush or continuous trickle of fluid from the vagina, which may indicate that the waters have broken. A noticeable reduction or change in the baby’s usual movement pattern. Pregnant women experiencing any of these symptoms should seek immediate assessment at a health facility. They should not wait at home for the symptoms to disappear. Early medical assessment is essential because timely intervention may help prevent complications or improve the baby’s chances of survival. CAN PRETERM BIRTH BE PREVENTED? Not all premature births can be prevented. However, certain measures can reduce the risk and improve outcomes for both mother and baby. MamaCare by Racheal is encouraging pregnant women to register for antenatal care early, preferably during the first trimester, and attend all recommended appointments. Other important measures include taking prescribed iron, folic acid and other supplements, eating a balanced diet, seeking prompt treatment for infections and having blood pressure and blood glucose levels monitored. Women should also avoid smoking, alcohol and harmful substances and inform their healthcare providers about any previous premature births or pregnancy complications. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A BABY IS BORN PREMATURELY? One of the most common challenges is Respiratory Distress Syndrome, which occurs when the baby’s lungs have not produced enough surfactant, a substance that helps keep the lungs open. Affected babies may struggle to breathe and require oxygen, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), or other forms of respiratory support. They may also experience hypothermia because their bodies have limited fat reserves and are not yet able to regulate temperature effectively. Feeding can be another challenge. Some premature babies have not developed the coordination required to suck, swallow and breathe properly. They may therefore need expressed breast milk through a feeding tube or other appropriate feeding support. Other complications include neonatal sepsis, jaundice and, in some cases, longer-term developmental challenges involving vision, hearing, movement, learning and overall development. CARE FOR PRETERM BABIES: THE IMPORTANCE OF KANGAROO MOTHER CARE The care given to a premature baby depends on the baby’s gestational age, NICU admissions, Kangaroo Mother Care(KMC), among others. KANGAROO MOTHER CARE: A LIFE-SAVING EMBRACE Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is an evidence-based method of caring for premature and low-birth-weight babies. It involves early, continuous and prolonged skin-to-skin contact between the baby and the mother or another caregiver, alongside appropriate breast milk feeding, preferably exclusive breastfeeding. The World Health Organization recommends Kangaroo Mother Care as routine care for all preterm and low-birth-weight babies. Its benefits include: Helping regulate the baby’s body temperature. Improving breastfeeding and feeding outcomes. Reducing the risk of infections. However, Kangaroo Mother Care does not replace essential medical treatment. Babies who require oxygen therapy, CPAP, incubator care, medication or specialised feeding support must continue receiving these interventions alongside KMC where clinically appropriate. WHEN SHOULD PARENTS SEEK IMMEDIATE MEDICAL ATTENTION? Difficulty or unusually fast breathing. Pauses in breathing. Chest indrawing or grunting. Blue or unusually pale lips and skin. Poor feeding or inability to feed. Fever or an abnormally low body temperature. Convulsions. Extreme sleepiness or difficulty waking. Reduced movement or unusual weakness. Yellow discolouration of the eyes or skin, particularly when it develops early, worsens or spreads. Preterm birth remains an important maternal and newborn health concern. Improving outcomes requires a collective commitment from healthcare professionals, policymakers, families and communities. As MamaCare by Racheal marks World Prematurity Month, the message is simple: every baby deserves a chance to survive and thrive, regardless of how early they arrive.

items.title: APC rally: Traders make brisk business in Ibadan, awaiting Tinubu’s arrival
items.description: Traders, on Saturday, ahead of the arrival of President Bola Tinubu for the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign at the historic Mapo Hall in Ibadan, made brisk business. Items which were majorly on sale were customised APC caps and T-shirts with different inscriptions, as well as sachet/table water, soft drinks and snacks. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the venue of the rally and its neighbourhood, such as Beere, Oja-Oba and Idi-Arere, were filled by thousands of APC members and supporters who came to hear from the number one citizen of Nigeria. Sellers of brooms, the symbol of the APC, also had a good business day, as did vendors selling kolanut and bitter kola. Some of the traders who spoke with NAN expressed satisfaction with the sales already recorded even before the start of the programme and arrival of President Bola Tinubu. Mrs Janet Yewande, a food vendor near the venue, said she hired an additional six people to cope with the high volume of people waiting to buy from her shop. She said that the high influx of customers had not made her increase the price or reduce the quantity of food. On her part, Miss Rasheedat Bolade said the extra sales being recorded in sachet water would go a long way in settling some pending bills and her school fees. Bolade said her mother had earlier bought enough bags of sachet water in preparation for the business of the day, adding that this had been her usual practice and means of survival whenever a big event was to be held at the ancient Mapo Hall. Also, Mr Akeem Ogunwale, who sold customised caps, also said that he had made the necessary preparations by printing more caps and T-shirts in anticipation of high sales. Ogunwale said that he had sold not less than 60 customised caps and 12 T-shirts at the campaign ground. A soft drink seller, Mrs Mercy Kingsley, said she had already sold 10 crates of soft drinks, noting that though many people preferred cold drinks due to the high intensity of the sun, they still went ahead to buy the ordinary ones due to high demand. A attendee at the campaign rally, Mr Kolade Ayinde, said the long hours in the sun compelled him to drink up to three sachets of water, adding that many supporters did not mind the intensity of the sun due to their love for the president. Ayinde said the presence of the traders was normal, as it met the needs of the party faithful, especially given the intensity of the sun. NAN reports that the mammoth crowd in and around Mapo Hall was still awaiting the arrival of the president and his team as of the time of filing this report. (NAN) The post APC rally: Traders make brisk business in Ibadan, awaiting Tinubu’s arrival appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ghana Prisons Service seeks reforms to strengthen inmate rehabilitation and reintegration
items.description: The Ghana Prisons Service has called for comprehensive reforms to strengthen its correctional system, improve inmate rehabilitation and reposition the institution as a key part of the country’s national security architecture. The call was made at the National Corrections Reform and Strategic Repositioning Forum held in Accra on Friday, November 20, 2026, as part of activities marking the 2026 Prisons and Corrections Month. The forum, held at the Ringway Assemblies of God Conference Auditorium, brought together experts and stakeholders to examine the Service’s operational systems and develop sustainable strategies to modernise correctional administration. Speaking at the event, the Director-General of Prisons, Mrs Patience Baffoe-Bonnie, Esq., said the role of corrections in national security made prison reform a collective responsibility. Addressing the forum under the theme, “Think Prisons 360 Degrees: Advancing Reforms, Changing Perceptions, and Transforming Lives”, she said the calibre of participants demonstrated that corrections was not merely an institutional concern but a national priority requiring collective expertise and decisive action. Mrs Baffoe-Bonnie outlined several initiatives undertaken by the Service to improve the welfare of officers and inmates, particularly in healthcare, education and access to justice. She highlighted a partnership with SIC to provide health insurance coverage for prison officers, as well as the introduction of a virtual psychosocial clinic to address mental healthcare needs. On inmate education, she disclosed that 63 inmates had earned university degrees, with several graduating with first-class honours. She also cited progress in justice delivery, including the pilot tele-hearing virtual court system at Ankaful, which is expected to improve access to judicial proceedings. The forum featured a panel discussion on the Service’s administrative structure, with experts proposing interventions to strengthen its operations and advance its reform agenda. The panel comprised retired Supreme Court Justice Jones V.M. Dotse; Dean of the University of Ghana School of Law, Prof. Raymond Atuguba; retired Deputy Director-General of Prisons in charge of Operations, DDGP (Rtd) Sylvester K.B. Rabbles; Democracy and Development Fellow at CDD-Ghana, Dr John Osae-Kwapong; Pro-Vice-Chancellor of the Ghana Communication Technology University, Prof. Robert E. Hinson; and legal practitioner and accredited public relations professional, Mr Jonah Eledi, Esq. The panellists called for a comprehensive national communication strategy to improve public understanding of the Service’s reformative mandate and reshape perceptions of prisons. They also recommended sustainable funding mechanisms, including public-private partnerships and dedicated statutory allocations, to provide the resources needed for inmate rehabilitation and long-term reintegration into society. Earlier, the Chairman of the Planning Committee and Commandant of the Prison Officers’ Training School, DDP Isaac Abuaku-Ameyaw, delivered an address titled “Who Pushed Me?” He described the forum as an important milestone in efforts to rethink corrections, drive bold institutional reforms, reshape public perceptions and secure a transformative future for the Ghana Prisons Service.

items.title: AG must publish quarterly figures on police detention breaches – Victoria Bright
items.description: International corporate lawyer and entrepreneur Victoria Bright has urged the Attorney General to publish quarterly reports detailing violations of the constitutional 48-hour detention limit by law enforcement officers, saying the move is necessary to ensure accountability under the new directive on arrest, detention and prosecution. She wants the reports to disclose the number of suspects held beyond the constitutionally permitted period, complaints upheld against officers and disciplinary measures taken against those found culpable. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mrs Bright said the directive must be assessed by its impact on police conduct and the consequences for officers who disregard the rights of suspects. “So what I would like to see now is accountability. I would ask that the Attorney General should publish anonymised figures by agencies showing as how many people were held beyond 48 hours in the quarter being reported on, how many complaints were upheld, what disciplinary action was taken or actions were taken against the officers who are involved. And if a breach is indeed established, the agency head must take disciplinary action and report what was done. “And if the evidence does point to an offense such as assault or extortion, investigate it and prosecute it where the evidence warrants it. And anyone who is unlawfully detained can go to court for release or seek compensation.” To strengthen monitoring, she proposed that quarterly compliance figures be checked against police custody records and court appearance times, with supervisors required to explain any breaches. Read also: Investigative agencies to face quarterly scrutiny over treatment of suspects – AG’s Office She also urged the Judicial Service to ensure that courts are available to hear cases when the 48-hour detention period expires on weekends. She said although the 48-hour detention rule has existed for decades, its enforcement remains a concern, particularly where suspects are arrested shortly before weekends. “If you are detained at four o’clock on Friday afternoon, the deadline is four o’clock on Sunday. The weekend thing has been long resolved by the Supreme Court,” she said. Mrs Bright stressed that the detention period must be calculated from the moment a person’s liberty is restricted, rather than when officers formally record the arrest at a police station. She welcomed the Attorney General’s directive, which took effect on November 2, but said its success would depend on whether law enforcement agencies comply with its provisions and take action against officers responsible for violations. “I judge it by two things: whether people are indeed released or brought before a judge on time, in accordance with their constitutional rights, one; and two, what actually ends up happening to these officers or supervisors when that fails,” she said. The directive also addresses other concerns surrounding arrests and detention, including coerced confessions, unlawful searches, mistreatment in custody and the denial of access to legal representation. It requires officers to inform suspects immediately, in a language they understand, of the reasons for their arrest and their right to a lawyer of their choice. Suspects who cannot afford legal representation must also be informed about the availability of legal aid. Mrs Bright further highlighted provisions requiring officers to document reasons for granting, refusing or imposing conditions on police bail, while prohibiting demands for money, gifts or favours in exchange for bail. She also called for an end to the use of police arrest and detention to compel people to settle civil debts, arguing that unpaid debt alone does not provide grounds for criminal arrest. Mrs Bright said the protection offered by the directive must extend to all citizens, regardless of their social standing or public profile. Her comments follow the Attorney General’s directive requiring law enforcement and investigative agencies to comply with the constitutional 48-hour detention limit and other safeguards protecting arrested persons. The directive applies to institutions including the Ghana Police Service, the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), the National Intelligence Bureau (NIB) and the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC). It requires arrested persons to be informed of the reasons for their arrest and their right to legal representation, while prohibiting the use of arrest and detention to recover civil debts. It also demands respect for suspects’ right to silence and voluntary confessions and prohibits unlawful searches, torture and coercion. The agencies are further required to submit quarterly compliance reports to the Attorney-General detailing arrests, releases, court appearances and alleged violations of suspects’ rights.

items.title: Une affaire de mœurs pose la question des libertés en Tunisie
items.description: La manière avec laquelle a été fuitée et traitée sur les réseaux sociaux l’affaire de «l’arrestation d’un député et d’une avocate pour prostitution dans un hôtel à La Marsa» pose de sérieuses questions sur l’état des libertés publiques et individuelles en Tunisie, d’autant que le nom du député en question a été donné en pâture à la vindicte populaire. Dans un commentaire publié sur Facebook, l’historien Abdeljalil Bouguerra constaté que les utilisateurs des réseaux sociaux ont continué de faire circuler la nouvelle pendant toute la journée d’hier, comme si cette affaire était devenue une priorité dans leur vie quotidienne, au point de faire abstraction de leur propre situation socio-économique du moment, qui n’est pas, on le sait, peu reluisante. «Indépendamment de la qualification juridique des faits impliquant le député et l’avocate — et abstraction faite de la formulation grossière, indécente et maladroite de l’information, qui rapporte qu’une ‘‘chambre d'hôtel à La Marsa a été prise d’assaut, menant à l’arrestation d’un député et d’une avocate pour prostitution’’ — ce qui s’est produit est extrêmement grave. Il s’agit d’un immense recul, d’une menace directe pesant sur les libertés individuelles et d’un signal d’une extrême négativité», a noté Abdeljalil Bouguerra. Et d’ajouter : «L’État doit clarifier ses choix, afin que le citoyen puisse comprendre ses droits et ses devoirs, et pour que le ‘‘contrat social’’ soit transparent et contraignant pour tous : Vivons-nous au sein d’un système religieux fermé, de type ‘‘taliban’’ — semblable à celui de l’Afghanistan — qui ne reconnaît ni les libertés publiques ni les libertés individuelles ? Ou bien au sein d’un système civil moderne qui respecte, à tout le moins, les libertés privées ? Et chacun se retrouve-t-il désormais dans une situation de ‘‘liberté provisoire’’ ?» I. B. L’article Une affaire de mœurs pose la question des libertés en Tunisie est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Identifiant unique: le ministère des Affaires étrangères marque son adhésion
items.description: ‎(Ouagadougou, 20 novembre 2026) Le personnel du ministère des Affaires étrangères s’est mobilisé ce 19 novembre, dans le cadre de l'opération nationale d'enrôlement à l'Identifiant Unique Electronique (IUE) de la personne physique au Burkina Faso. ‎Prévue du 19 au 20 novembre 2026 au sein de ministère cette mobilisation traduit l'adhésion du département de la diplomatie burkinabè à une réforme majeure visant à moderniser l'administration publique et à renforcer la fiabilité des données relatives aux personnes physiques. ‎Donnant l'exemple, le Camarade ministre des Affaires étrangères, le Camarade Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE et la Camarade ministre déléguée, Stella Eldine KABRE/KABORE, se sont soumis à la procédure d'enrôlement, en fournissant leurs données biographiques et biométriques. ‎À cette occasion, le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè a salué la mise en œuvre de cette initiative, tout en invitant l'ensemble du personnel à se mobiliser pour se prêter à l’exercice, et ainsi s'inscrire pleinement dans la vision de refondation de l'État impulsée par le Camarade Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORE, qui fait de la modernisation de l'administration publique, de la transformation numérique et de l'amélioration de la gouvernance des leviers essentiels de la Révolution Progressiste Populaire. ‎En rappel, l’opération d’enregistrement de masse de la population au Registre de l’identifiant unique s’est tenue ce mercredi 11 novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, sous le patronage du président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim TRAORE. Cette opération vise à attribuer à chaque Burkinabè et à toute personne étrangère vivant ou en transit au Burkina Faso, un identifiant unique électronique de la personne physique (IUE). Pour le gouvernement, il s’agit de permettre à l’Etat de connaître avec davantage de précision les personnes vivant sur son territoire, de mieux organiser ses interventions et de garantir une identification fiable de chaque citoyen et résident. ‎A ce titre, l'identifiant unique constitue un instrument stratégique pour améliorer la connaissance des ressources humaines, faciliter les procédures administratives et assurer une meilleure planification des politiques publiques. ‎‎DCRP/MAE L’article Identifiant unique: le ministère des Affaires étrangères marque son adhésion est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: NaCCA urges international schools to integrate Ghanaian values into curricula
items.description: The National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NaCCA) has urged international curriculum providers and schools operating in Ghana to incorporate Ghanaian cultural values and local contexts into their teaching programmes. The Council says that while international curricula offer learners valuable global exposure, it is important that students also understand Ghanaian culture, values and heritage. Speaking to the media at the Pearson Learner Awards 2026, the Deputy Director-General of NaCCA in charge of Technical Services, Dr Eric Amoah, commended schools and learners for their outstanding achievements, particularly one school that received about 26 awards. He also praised teachers for their dedication and commitment to academic excellence, urging learners to work harder to achieve even greater success in future editions of the awards. The Pearson Learner Awards recognise top-performing international students outside the UK who achieve outstanding examination results in Pearson Edexcel qualifications. Winners are notified through their schools in November 2026, based on results from the previous October, January and May/June examination series. On the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education, Dr Amoah said AI had come to stay and must be embraced by the country’s education system. He said the ongoing curriculum review, covering Kindergarten to Primary Six, places significant emphasis on Artificial Intelligence, coding, computational thinking, and robotics. He, however, cautioned that learners must be guided on the responsible use of AI, particularly in developing appropriate prompts and ensuring that the technology supports rather than undermines their learning. Dr Amoah further stressed the need to equip teachers with the necessary skills to integrate AI into lesson planning and classroom instruction as Ghana moves towards a technology-driven education system. Out of the 34 awards presented at the ceremony, Accra-based Crystal Heights International School secured 26, while the remaining eight were shared among other participating schools in Ghana. The school’s impressive haul comprised 12 Highest Mark in the World awards and 14 Highest Mark in Africa awards, highlighting its growing reputation for academic excellence. The award recipients were among more than 2,700 learners from 740 schools across 85 countries who qualified for recognition following the 2025/2026 Pearson Edexcel examinations. Speaking on the school’s achievement, Daniel Lomotey Nartey, Principal in charge of the Pearson Division at Crystal Heights International School, expressed excitement over the performance, attributing the success to the collective efforts of school management, teachers, parents and learners. He commended the school’s management for investing in infrastructure, providing essential teaching and learning resources, and ensuring that teachers receive the necessary support to deliver quality education. Mr Nartey also acknowledged the significant contribution of parents, particularly their commitment to providing learning materials, participating in parent-teacher engagements, and implementing recommendations from teachers to enhance their children’s academic development. On the school’s approach to Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education, Mr Nartey disclosed that Crystal Heights International School has a dedicated robotics laboratory, supported by trained teachers who provide learners with practical learning experiences. He explained that the initiative enables students to apply classroom knowledge to real-life situations rather than relying solely on memorisation. For instance, mathematical concepts such as measurement, area and volume are applied in designing and creating objects in the robotics laboratory. The school believes that this hands-on approach is helping learners develop critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving and innovation skills. Mr Nartey said the achievement of the 26 learners reflected the school’s commitment to academic excellence and practical, skills-based education. Meanwhile, Pearson has reaffirmed its commitment to promoting the responsible and safe integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education, emphasising the importance of keeping teachers at the centre of the learning process. Speaking on the sidelines of the Pearson Learner Awards 2026 in Ghana, Lisa Evans, Global Marketing Director and Sales Director for Africa, Europe and the Americas at Pearson, said AI presented both exciting opportunities and challenges for learners worldwide. She stressed that although AI was transforming education, its application must be guided by teachers to ensure that technology supports, rather than replaces, the role of educators. According to her, Pearson is working closely with global education experts and institutions, including UNESCO and the Department for Education, to ensure that AI-powered learning resources and assessment systems prioritise teacher leadership and learner safety. Reflecting on the achievements of the award recipients, Ms Evans described the ceremony as a remarkable celebration of academic excellence. She noted that the awards went beyond recognising learners who attained the highest marks nationally, regionally and globally, adding that they also celebrated the hard work, resilience, dedication and determination demonstrated by the students. She further acknowledged the important roles played by parents, teachers, school administrators and support staff in helping learners achieve their academic ambitions. The Pearson Learner Awards continue to provide international recognition for outstanding academic performance, celebrating learners whose achievements demonstrate excellence and dedication to education.

items.title: Ga West Education Directorate celebrates International Children’s Day, calls for greater protection of children’s rights
items.description: The Ga West Education Directorate has joined the global community to celebrate International Children’s Day, calling on parents, teachers and caregivers to provide safe, inclusive and supportive environments that promote the holistic development of children. The Deputy Director of Early Childhood Education at the Ga West Education Directorate, Mrs Jemima Dufie Agyepong, said the celebration provided an opportunity to recognise the potential of children and renew the collective commitment to protecting their rights and supporting their growth. In her address, she highlighted the importance of early childhood education in shaping children’s character, creativity and lifelong learning abilities, noting that the early years were crucial for developing essential values and skills such as patience, kindness, resilience and self-confidence. Mrs Agyepong encouraged children to remain curious, ask questions and express themselves freely, stressing that their opinions and voices must be respected and valued. She also commended early childhood educators and caregivers for their dedication, emphasising that their responsibilities extended beyond teaching literacy and numeracy to providing emotional support and creating opportunities for children to discover and develop their abilities. She called for stronger collaboration among parents, families and schools, explaining that effective partnerships between the home and the classroom were essential to raising confident, responsible and compassionate children. The Deputy Director further urged stakeholders to protect children’s right to play, ensure that their right to be heard was respected and provide learning environments where every child, regardless of background or ability, felt safe, respected and valued. She commended the management and staff of Linvoy Academy, particularly the school administrator, Madam Rose Appiah, for promoting holistic education through academic activities, cultural engagement, character development and physical well-being. The celebration featured a variety of activities, including poetry recitals, drama performances, choreography and an exhibition of egg-based dishes prepared by parents, teachers and pupils. The event also highlighted the importance of child nutrition, with a call on stakeholders to work together to improve children’s nutritional well-being and support institutions committed to child-centred education. International Children’s Day is observed annually on November 20 to promote children’s rights, welfare and well-being. The day commemorates the adoption of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989 and the Declaration of the Rights of the Child in 1959. The celebration provides an opportunity to amplify children’s voices, recognise their concerns and encourage their participation in conversations and decisions that affect their lives and future. The occasion serves as a reminder that investing in children’s health, education, nutrition and overall development is essential to building a brighter, safer and more inclusive future.

items.title: ‘I’ll be back’: vows Kane after ankle surgery
items.description: Bayern Munich’s star striker Harry Kane pledged to return for the “business end of the season” after undergoing surgery on his left ankle on Saturday. Kane limped off after 20 minutes of Bayern’s 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday, the club confirming the England captain had torn a ligament in his ankle. Bayern issued a statement Saturday saying the Ballon d’Or winner had “successfully undergone surgery” on his left ankle. “The 33-year-old will now begin his rehabilitation program,” Bayern said, with the injury expected to keep Kane out for three to four months. Kane posted a picture on social media from his hospital bed on Saturday, vowing to work his way back to fitness this season. “The highs and lows of life! Obviously very disappointed to get this injury but as always it’s an opportunity to show resilience and improvement going into 2027. “I’ll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season.” Kane shared a quote from three-time Super Bowl-winning wide receiver Julian Edelman: “tough times don’t last, tough people do”, while thanking his supporters for their messages of support. Kane has a history of ankle issues although he has only missed a handful of games since moving to Bayern in 2023. England coach Thomas Tuchel will be keeping a keen eye out on how England’s most capped player’s rehabilitation progresses. England play Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in late March. The injury comes at a difficult time for Bayern, who are currently missing several players, particularly up front. Bayern are without Luis Diaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and captain Manuel Neuer, while midfielder Jamal Musiala and coach Vincent Kompany both returned after long lay-offs on Friday. The post ‘I’ll be back’: vows Kane after ankle surgery appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: « En 2026, la situation globale des évaluations menées par l’ANAQ-Sup traduit une consolidation majeure du dispositif d’assurance qualité au Sénégal »
items.description: En 2026, au Sénégal, la situation globale des évaluations menées par l’Autorité nationale d’Assurance Qualité de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la recherche et de l’innovation (ANAQ-Sup) traduit une consolidation majeure du dispositif d'assurance qualité à travers le pays. C’est ce qu’a indiqué son Secrétaire exécutif, le Professeur Massamba Diouf, dans un entretien accordé au Soleil. D’ailleurs, informe-t-il, en fin d’année, il est attendu une continuité et une accélération des évaluations institutionnelles, de programmes de formation, d’écoles doctorales et de centres de recherche. Dans le paysage de l'enseignement supérieur au Sénégal (public et privé), on observe souvent une confusion entre l'habilitation et l'accréditation. Pouvez-vous expliquer clairement la différence entre ces deux procédures ? Dans le dispositif national d’assurance qualité de l’enseignement supérieur au Sénégal, l’habilitation est relative à l’EES et l’accréditation au diplôme. Elles constituent les deux critères de reconnaissance des diplômes délivrés par les EES publics et privés. Elles sont complémentaires mais distinctes par leur objet, leur portée et leurs finalités. L’habilitation vise l’établissement. C’est l’autorisation donnée par le ministère de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation (MESRI) à un établissement d’enseignement supérieur pour délivrer des diplômes. Elle est obligatoire pour tous les établissements qui délivrent des diplômes au format LMD (Licence, Master, Doctorat). Elle est accordée par arrêté du ministre, après une évaluation de l’offre de formation par l’Autorité nationale d’assurance qualité de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la recherche et de l’innovation (ANAQ-Sup). Elle est valable pour une durée de dix (10) ans. La procédure doit commencer après un an d’ouverture. A lire aussi : Enseignement supérieur : vers la mise en place d’un Cadre national des qualifications du Sénégal L’accréditation vise un programme de formation. C’est un processus d’évaluation et d’examen qui permet d’attester qu’un programme précis répond aux normes, standards et critères de qualité fixés par les référentiels de l’ANAQ-Sup. Elle est valable pour une durée de cinq ans. La procédure doit être entamée après la sortie d’une promotion de licence, de master et de doctorat. En définitive, la distinction fondamentale peut être résumée de la manière suivante. L’habilitation reconnaît la capacité d’un établissement à délivrer des diplômes de l’enseignement supérieur, tandis que l’accréditation reconnaît la qualité d’un programme de formation conduisant à un diplôme donné. Un établissement habilité ne dispose donc pas automatiquement de l'accréditation de tous ses programmes de formation. Laquelle de ces deux processus est indispensable, et comment s'articulent-ils dans le dispositif global d'assurance qualité de l'ANAQ-Sup ? Il convient de préciser d’emblée que l'habilitation et l'accréditation ne sont pas des processus concurrents, mais deux exigences complémentaires qui participent à la crédibilité et à la qualité des diplômes et du système d'enseignement supérieur sénégalais. La reconnaissance d’un diplôme, c’est l’acceptation formelle par l’État. Elle donne des droits, des privilèges et des prérogatives à son titulaire qui peut ainsi prétendre à des postes ou participer à des concours ouverts par l’État. La reconnaissance confère aussi les droits en matière de poursuite d’études ou d’insertion professionnelle, y compris dans le cadre de la mobilité nationale et internationale. Dans le sous-secteur de l’enseignement supérieur, la reconnaissance des diplômes est régie par le décret nᵒ 2015-582 du 11 mai 2015 relatif à la reconnaissance, au classement et à l’équivalence des diplômes de l’enseignement supérieur, modifié en 2021 et en 2026. En résumé, selon ce décret, pour être reconnu, un diplôme doit remplir deux conditions. D’une part, il doit être délivré par un établissement d’enseignement supérieur habilité ou agréé par le ministère de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation (MESRI). D’autre part il doit être accrédité par l’ANAQ-Sup ou reconnu par le CAMES. Toutefois, il faut noter que tout diplôme ne peut être soumis à la reconnaissance du CAMES s’il n’est pas reconnu au Sénégal (EES habilité et diplôme accrédité). Pourquoi certains programmes de formation au sein des établissements d'enseignement supérieur (EES) perdent-ils leur accréditation et habilitation au fil du temps ? Il est important de préciser que l’habilitation et l’accréditation ne sont pas des reconnaissances acquises définitivement. Elles s'inscrivent dans une logique d'assurance qualité et d'amélioration continue. Il convient toutefois de distinguer deux situations : l'arrivée à échéance normale de la période de validité et la remise en cause de la reconnaissance pour non-conformité aux exigences de qualité. L'habilitation et l'accréditation sont accordées pour des durées déterminées. Selon les informations publiées par l'ANAQ-Sup, l'habilitation a une durée de validité de dix ans, tandis que l'accréditation des programmes est valable cinq ans. À l'expiration de ces périodes, l'établissement ou le programme doit faire l'objet d'une nouvelle évaluation pour obtenir le renouvellement de la reconnaissance concernée. L'expiration d'une accréditation ne signifie donc pas nécessairement que la qualité du programme s'est dégradée. Elle traduit d'abord la fin de la période pour laquelle la conformité du programme avait été officiellement attestée. Une nouvelle évaluation devient nécessaire pour vérifier que les exigences de qualité continuent d'être respectées. Lorsqu'un programme d’un établissement ou une habilitation arrive à terme, quelles sont les démarches pour les recouvrer ? L'établissement doit assurer le suivi de la durée de validité de ses reconnaissances et anticiper leur renouvellement, afin d'éviter toute interruption de leur validité. L'établissement manifeste son intérêt auprès de l'ANAQ-Sup dans le cadre des appels à manifestation d'intérêt ou selon les modalités de programmation applicables à la procédure concernée. L'établissement procède à une analyse approfondie de sa situation à partir du référentiel d'évaluation correspondant. Il élabore un rapport d'auto-évaluation étayé par des éléments de preuve, en accordant une attention particulière à la mise en œuvre des recommandations précédentes. Une équipe d'experts indépendants, mobilisée par l'ANAQ-Sup, examine le rapport d'auto-évaluation et réalise une visite destinée à apprécier la conformité de l'établissement ou du programme aux standards de qualité. Le rapport d'évaluation externe est soumis au Conseil scientifique de l'ANAQ-Sup, qui examine les résultats, délibère et se prononce sur la procédure. En matière d'accréditation, la décision est prise par le Conseil scientifique. Pour l'habilitation, le Conseil scientifique émet un avis technique sur lequel repose l'acte administratif délivré par le ministère chargé de l'Enseignement supérieur (arrêté). Ces étapes correspondent à l'architecture générale du dispositif d'évaluation de l'ANAQ-Sup. En cette année 2026, quel bilan dressez-vous concernant la situation globale des habilitations et des accréditations dans l'ensemble des EES publics et privés du Sénégal ? En 2026, la situation globale des évaluations menées par l'ANAQ-Sup traduit une consolidation majeure du dispositif d'assurance qualité au Sénégal. Le nombre cumulé est de 721 évaluations externes réalisées dans le secteur privé et 323 dans le public, soit un total de 1044 depuis la création de l’ANAQ-Sup. De façon désagrégée, les 721 évaluations dans le privé sont constituées de 226 évaluations institutionnelles (habilitation) ayant donné lieu à 164 avis favorables et 62 défavorables, et 495 évaluations de programmes (accréditation) ayant débouché sur 315 décisions d’accréditation. Quant aux 323 évaluations réalisées dans le secteur public, il est à noter 12 évaluations institutionnelles (habilitation) qui ont abouti à 100 % d’avis favorables et 311 programmes évalués (accréditation) pour 267 décisions d’accréditation. Cette dynamique s'est intensifiée en 2025 avec l'évaluation de 3 écoles doctorales et d'un centre de recherche. Fin 2026, il est attendu une continuité et une accélération des évaluations institutionnelles, de programmes de formation, d’écoles doctorales et de centres de recherche. Une des innovations majeures introduites dans les évaluations est la dématérialisation quasi-totale des procédures d’évaluation avec la plateforme « E-ANAQ ». Quels sont aujourd'hui les principaux défis à relever pour garantir un pilotage efficace de l'assurance qualité et résoudre la problématique de la conformité des offres de formation dans l'enseignement supérieur ? Le principal défi est aujourd’hui la montée en puissance de l’ANAQ-Sup qui devra passer par une augmentation significative de son budget et de ses ressources humaines pour couvrir l’ensemble des EES, des programmes de formation, des écoles doctorales et des centres de recherche. Il est également important de soutenir et de pérenniser l’ancrage de la culture de la qualité au sein des établissements d’enseignement supérieur publics et privés. Cela passe par une meilleure appropriation des mécanismes d’assurance qualité internes, le renforcement des compétences des acteurs et une plus grande couverture des évaluations et des accréditations avec la dynamique de dématérialisation à poursuivre. Il est également essentiel que les recommandations issues des évaluations externes se traduisent en actions d’amélioration concrètes. L’ANAQ-Sup entend enfin renforcer ses actions d’accompagnement vis-à-vis des parties prenantes de l’enseignement supérieur mais aussi améliorer l’appui destiné à la communauté. L’enjeu est donc de dépasser une approche centrée sur la conformité pour faire de la qualité une conscience collective et une responsabilité partagée par les différents acteurs et intégrée à la gouvernance et au fonctionnement quotidien des établissements. Propos recueillis par Mariama DIEME

items.title: UGEL hostel charges among lowest compared to private facilities – Prof Abekah-Nkrumah
items.description: The University of Ghana says accommodation fees charged by the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL) remain among the lowest compared to privately operated hostels, despite concerns over the recent increase. Director of Institutional Advancement at the University of Ghana and member of the university’s Communications Team, Prof. Gordon Abekah-Nkrumah, says the charges reflect the cost of maintaining the facilities and providing additional services to students. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, he explained that the GH¢8,050 fee covers accommodation for two semesters, representing 32 weeks, and translates into approximately GH¢35.40 per day. He said the amount covers more than just the use of a room, as UGEL also provides electricity, running water, drinking water, sanitation and other essential services. “The package is that you have that room. You have electricity, and electricity is on cap,” he said. Prof. Abekah-Nkrumah explained that, unlike some privately operated hostels where students are required to pay separately for electricity after exhausting a limited allocation, UGEL provides electricity within a capped arrangement. He added that the company also bears the cost of running water, supplies drinking water and provides students with a pack of tissue every semester. UGEL, he said, is additionally responsible for sanitation, maintenance of the hostel compounds and the provision of pastoral services, including the payment of tutors who support students in the residential facilities. He argued that these services, alongside administrative and operational expenses, must be considered when assessing whether the accommodation charges are expensive. “So I think that is important for us to understand when we say it is expensive. Expensive against what?” he questioned.”And so if you look at what we have right now, it’s probably among the private hostels. It is the cheapest.” On the 15 per cent adjustment from the initially proposed 26 per cent increase, Prof. Abekah-Nkrumah said the reduction was the outcome of negotiations between the university and the Residency Board, which includes student representatives. He rejected suggestions that the reduction resulted from the intervention of the Rent Commissioner, Frederick Opoku, insisting that it followed the university’s internal consultation process. He further explained that UGEL was established as a wholly owned subsidiary of the University of Ghana following challenges in financing the construction and management of additional student accommodation. According to him, the university had resorted to commercial borrowing from six banks to address a severe accommodation shortage, which at the time forced several students to share rooms designed for fewer occupants. He warned that failure to meet the loan repayment obligations could expose the hostel facilities, which serve as collateral for the loans, to takeover by the banks. “If we can’t pay the loans, remember those buildings are collateral to the loan. And so the banks can step in and take over the properties,” he said. Prof. Abekah-Nkrumah maintained that the university was also conscious of students who could not afford the charges and had made financial assistance available through its Student Financial Aid Office, including support for accommodation. His comments come amid ongoing concerns over the affordability of university accommodation and the recent disagreement between UGEL and the Rent Commissioner over hostel charges.

A-G’s directive on suspects’ rights must translate into action, not just promises – Sulemana Braimah
items.description: The Executive Director of the Media Foundation for West Africa (MFWA), Sulemana Braimah, has cautioned that the Attorney-General’s directive on protecting the rights of arrested persons must be backed by effective enforcement to produce meaningful results. He said although the directive reinforces important constitutional and legal safeguards, its success would depend on whether law enforcement agencies translate the requirements into their daily operations. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mr Braimah welcomed the directive, describing decisions aimed at promoting and protecting people’s rights as fundamental. However, he questioned why law enforcement agencies had, over the years, failed to consistently uphold requirements that were already captured in existing laws. The Attorney-General’s directive requires law enforcement and investigative agencies, including the Ghana Police Service, the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), the National Intelligence Bureau (NIB) and the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC), to comply with the constitutional 48-hour detention limit and other safeguards protecting suspects. It also requires arrested persons to be informed of the reasons for their arrest and their right to legal representation, while prohibiting the use of arrest and detention to recover civil debts, unlawful searches, torture and coercion. The agencies are further required to respect suspects’ right to silence and ensure that confessions are voluntary, while submitting quarterly compliance reports to the Attorney-General detailing arrests, releases, court appearances and alleged rights violations. Mr Braimah said the directive was a welcome development but warned against allowing it to become another official declaration that generates public expectations without producing tangible changes. “The challenge is whether or not it is going to be one of those usual things where nice policy statements are made, nice declarations and directives are issued and at the end of the day we are just back to square one,” he said. He argued that the real achievement would be seen when citizens begin to experience improved protection of their rights in their dealings with law enforcement agencies. Drawing a comparison with political party manifestoes, he said governments often presented attractive promises and policies but failed to deliver the expected changes after assuming office. Mr Braimah therefore maintained that the Attorney-General’s directive should be judged by its practical outcomes rather than the announcement itself. He also acknowledged that enforcing the requirements could prove more difficult in practice than it appeared on paper, making sustained commitment from the affected institutions essential. He stressed that while the directive deserved recognition, meaningful acknowledgement would only be justified when its implementation began to produce visible results for the protection of citizens’ rights.

items.title: Catholic Church in Nigeria has supported me spiritually, financially – Jude Nnam
items.description: Renowned Nigerian composer, singer and music director, Dr Jude Nnam, has acknowledged the financial and spiritual support he has received from the Catholic Church in Nigeria during his ongoing medical treatment in India. Nnam, who is currently recuperating, said the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria (CBCN) had been instrumental in supporting him throughout his medical journey, contrary to suggestions by some individuals that the Church had not done enough to assist him. In a message of appreciation to friends and supporters on his Facebook page, the music director said he was getting better by the day through God’s grace, prayers and support from the Church and well-wishers. Addressing concerns raised by some individuals over the need for the Catholic Church in Nigeria to assist with the financial burden of his treatment, Nnam said the Church had provided him with tremendous support. He particularly expressed gratitude to the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria for taking responsibility for his situation and providing both financial and spiritual assistance since his arrival in India. Nnam also singled out the Secretary-General of the Catholic Secretariat of Nigeria, Rev. Fr. Michael Banjo, for his personal commitment and support. According to him, Banjo visited him in India on behalf of the Bishops Conference, bringing gifts and blessings from the bishops, and spent an entire week with him. He said the priest celebrated Mass for him daily throughout his stay before returning to Nigeria. The composer further acknowledged the individual contributions of Catholic bishops and dioceses, noting that they had supported him through telephone calls, messages and financial contributions. He also thanked friends and other well-wishers whose prayers and financial contributions had helped sustain him during the challenging period. “Be rest assured that the Catholic Church in Nigeria has supported me in this journey in no small measure, and I remain grateful,” he said. Nnam appealed for continued prayers for his recovery, expressing optimism that he would soon return to Nigeria and resume his musical and religious assignments. “By the grace of God, I shall be back soon to continue the work of my Father and my Healer,” he said. The post Catholic Church in Nigeria has supported me spiritually, financially – Jude Nnam appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Enseignement supérieur : 96 640 nouveaux bacheliers pour seulement 57 000 places
items.description: L’enseignement supérieur sénégalais fait face à une forte pression sur ses capacités d’accueil. Pour cette rentrée 2026-2027, avec 96 640 nouveaux bacheliers et près de 94 000 demandes d’orientation enregistrées, seulement 57 000 places sont disponibles. Le défi s’annonce considérable. Lors du Conseil interministériel consacré à la rentrée 2026-2027, le ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur, Boubacar Camara, a exposé les difficultés et les mesures envisagées pour faire face à la massification des effectifs. L’afflux de nouveaux bacheliers constitue l’un des principaux défis de la rentrée universitaire 2026-2027. Les établissements publics d’enseignement supérieur devront faire face à une demande d’orientation largement supérieure à leurs capacités d’accueil. Une situation qui remet au premier plan la problématique de la surcharge des universités, du déficit d’infrastructures pédagogiques et de l’insuffisance des moyens d’encadrement. Devant le Premier ministre Ahmadou Alhaminou Lô, lors du Conseil interministériel consacré à la rentrée, le ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation, Boubacar Camara, a présenté des chiffres révélateurs. Sur les 96 640 nouveaux bacheliers attendus, 94 000 demandes d’orientation ont déjà été enregistrées. Pourtant, les capacités disponibles sont estimées à seulement 57 000 places. L’écart entre les demandes enregistrées et les capacités annoncées atteint ainsi 37 000 places. Un déficit qui illustre les difficultés auxquelles les pouvoirs publics devront apporter des réponses pour garantir aux nouveaux bacheliers la possibilité de poursuivre leurs études. Face à cette situation, Boubacar Camara a annoncé une décision gouvernementale portant sur 50 000 places destinées aux universités. A lire aussi : Direction de l’Enseignement supérieur : les priorités du Directeur général, le Pr Mamadou Sidibé Cette mesure doit contribuer à organiser l’accueil des nouveaux étudiants. Toutefois, les modalités précises de cette allocation et son articulation avec les capacités existantes restent à clarifier. La question des places disponibles renvoie directement au déficit d’infrastructures universitaires. Malgré les investissements consentis, les établissements continuent de subir une pression croissante sur leurs amphithéâtres, leurs salles de travaux dirigés et leurs équipements pédagogiques. Le ministre a particulièrement insisté sur l’accélération des chantiers universitaires. Selon lui, certains projets de construction, engagés depuis 2015 ou 2017, ne sont toujours pas achevés alors que des financements existent. Une situation qui ralentit l’extension des capacités d’accueil. Le département de l’Enseignement supérieur entend travailler avec le ministère chargé des Infrastructures pour accélérer la livraison des ouvrages. Les investissements concernent aussi bien les infrastructures pédagogiques que les équipements sociaux, notamment les résidences universitaires et les structures de restauration. L’augmentation des effectifs pose également la question de l’encadrement pédagogique. Boubacar Camara a reconnu la nécessité de renforcer les ressources humaines pour maintenir un taux d’encadrement acceptable. Le recours à des enseignants vacataires figure parmi les solutions envisagées, en attendant des mesures plus durables. À la surcharge des universités s’ajoute le problème récurrent du calendrier académique. Les grèves, les retards dans les orientations et les difficultés d’organisation ont progressivement entraîné un chevauchement des années universitaires. Cette situation complique l’accueil des nouvelles promotions puisque certains étudiants poursuivent encore leurs enseignements lorsque les nouveaux bacheliers doivent intégrer les établissements. Elle exerce également une pression sur les bourses, les logements et les finances universitaires. Pour y remédier, le ministre a annoncé un plan de transition et de régularisation du calendrier académique. Des financements sont prévus dans le cadre des contrats de performance afin de permettre aux universités de retrouver progressivement un fonctionnement normal. Par Daouda DIOUF

items.title: Tourisme : l’Algérie vise 8 millions de visiteurs en 2029 et mobilise sa diaspora
items.description: L’Algérie actionne le moteur de la croissance que représente le tourisme et compte sur sa diaspora pour le développer avec un objectif tracé d’attirer 8 millions de touristes à l’horizon 2029. Pour cela, la ministre du Tourisme et de l’artisanat, Houria Medahi et le secrétaire d'État auprès du ministre des Affaires étrangères, chargé de la communauté nationale à l'étranger, Sofiane Chaib, a présidé jeudi une réunion avec des opérateurs économiques, des investisseurs, des acteurs du secteur touristique, des porteurs de projets et des représentants de startups issus de notre communauté nationale à l'étranger. Le délégué général de l'Association des banques et établissements financiers (ABEF), le Directeur général adjoint du Groupe public Hôtellerie, tourisme et thermalisme (GHTT), le Directeur général de l'Agence nationale du foncier touristique (ANFT), ainsi qu'un représentant de la Direction générale des Domaines nationaux, une représentante de l'Agence algérienne de promotion de l'investissement (AAPI) ont assisté à la réunion. Les chefs des postes consulaires d’Algérie à Paris, Marseille, Strasbourg, Genève, Bruxelles et Metz étaient également présents, selon un communiqué du ministère. Le tourisme constitue désormais « l'un des piliers fondamentaux de la diversification économique, ainsi qu'un levier de création de richesse et d’emplois », a dit la ministre, en ajoutant que son secteur s'inscrit dans une vision stratégique « ambitieuse, visant à accueillir 8 millions de touristes à l'horizon 2029 » et à « renforcer les capacités d'hébergement touristique, en adéquation avec les atouts exceptionnels dont regorge notre pays. » Tourisme : l’Algérie appelle sa diaspora à s’impliquer Mme Meddahi a ensuite évoqué les opportunités d’investissement dans le tourisme en Algérie. Elle a cité la réalisation et le développement d'établissements hôteliers et de structures d'hébergement ; le tourisme saharien, de montagne, écologique, culturel et spirituel ; le tourisme thermal et de bien-être ; les villages touristiques et les espaces de loisirs ; ainsi que le transport touristique, les services numériques et les applications intelligentes, la valorisation des produits du terroir et de l'artisanat, avec leur intégration aux circuits et destinations touristiques. Dans la foulée, la ministre du Tourisme et de l’Artisanat a demandé aux membres de la diaspora algérienne à « s'impliquer dans cette dynamique ». Elle a précisé que cette contribution « ne se limite pas au seul investissement financier ». L’Algérie veut impliquer sa diaspora dans le « transfert d'expertises et de connaissances, le développement de méthodes de gestion modernes, la promotion de l'innovation et de la numérisation, l'établissement de partenariats avec des opérateurs internationaux, l'attraction de tour-opérateurs, ainsi que la promotion de la destination Algérie sur les marchés étrangers. » Elle veut en faire de « véritables partenaires » dans l'édification d'un tourisme algérien compétitif et qui se distingue par son excellence. L’article Tourisme : l'Algérie vise 8 millions de visiteurs en 2029 et mobilise sa diaspora est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: High Court rules that Anlo Traditional Council lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate Atorkor chieftaincy dispute
items.description: The Denu High Court has ruled that the Anlo Traditional Council lacks jurisdiction over a chieftaincy dispute concerning the legitimate Dufia (Paramount Chief) for the Atorkor community in the Anloga District of the Volta Region. The Court, presided over by His Lordship Sylvester Nii Okai Ablor, also quashed a ruling that identified Torgbi Ackumey Geli Adjorlolo III of the Adjorlolo family as the legitimate Dufia (Paramount chief) for Atorkor. The Court directed the Kome-Shime Traditional Council to adjudicate the dispute and find a lasting solution, since the division falls within its jurisdiction. Background In May 2026, Torgbi Dosu Adaku VIII, through his lawyer, Torgbiga Wenya III (E. A. Vordoagu Esq.), sought legal redress at the Denu Court against a ruling by a judicial panel constituted by the Anlo Traditional Council. They argued that the Kome-Shime Traditional Area has the legitimate right to determine a chieftaincy status and succession case involving the Dosu Adaku Stool and Ackumey Geli Adjorlolo Stool, which fall within its jurisdiction. They further stated that Torgbi Samlafo IV, who presided over the panel, is a chief in the Avenor Traditional Area, which is outside the Anlo Traditional Council. They therefore asserted that the panel lacked “the legal competence and statutory authority” to adjudicate the case, since some members had been erroneously empanelled. Counsel for the applicants also indicated that Kome-Shime is a “separate, distinct and independent” traditional area and has been allocated traditional council status; therefore, its functional Judicial Committee has the power to adjudicate chieftaincy disputes. They asked the court to quash the ruling, arguing that the Anlo Traditional Council lacked the power to determine a dispute that arose outside its jurisdiction. The court granted the application on 18th November, 2026.

items.title: 2027: We’re not joining your opposition coalition, PDP tells Lukman
items.description: …Snubs November 30 summit, declares Wike’s Rainbow alliance its only coalition By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) has rejected claims that it has joined the opposition Coalition for Democracy being promoted by former National Vice Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Salihu Lukman, declaring that it will not attend the coalition’s November 30 summit. The party said it had not entered into any alliance with the coalition, authorised anyone to represent it at the summit or agreed to be bound by any decision taken in its name. It maintained that its only recognised coalition arrangement was the Rainbow Coalition, backed by its National Leader, Nyesom Wike. The position was contained in a statement signed by the PDP National Publicity Secretary, Hon. Jungudo Haruna Mohammed, who said those being presented as the party’s representatives were expelled members with no authority to speak or act on its behalf. Jungudo said the individuals’ claims to the party’s leadership and representation had suffered defeats at the Federal High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court. He added that the courts had issued orders restraining Kabiru Tanimu Turaki, SAN, and his associates from parading themselves as PDP leaders, while imposing financial penalties exceeding N100 million over alleged abuses of court processes and frivolous litigation. Questioning Lukman’s continued engagement with the individuals, Jungudo said, “It is therefore astonishing that Mr Salihu Lukman, who ought to be sufficiently informed about the legal status and recognised leadership of the PDP, would continue to engage these individuals and use them as a basis for associating the party with his so-called Toronto Coalition.” Describing the proposed arrangement as a political project built on misrepresentation, the PDP declared it ‘dead on arrival’, particularly because those being presented as its representatives lacked the authority to speak on its behalf. The party also threatened legal action against Lukman, his associates and other promoters of the Coalition for Democracy if they continued to use its name and institutional identity in their political activities. “The party will not hesitate to pursue appropriate legal action against any person or group that continues to unlawfully associate the PDP with this arrangement,” Jungudo warned. Reiterating its position, the party said the Rainbow Coalition, in line with Wike’s political direction and directives, remained its only recognised coalition arrangement. It consequently urged Nigerians, political stakeholders, members and supporters, as well as media organisations, to disregard reports linking its national headquarters at Wadata Plaza, Abuja, to the November 30 summit or any other political arrangement being promoted by Lukman and his associates. “The PDP will not allow its identity to be hijacked, its institutional authority misrepresented or its political interests compromised by individuals who have no mandate to speak or act on its behalf,” Jungudo said. The party maintained that it would not be bound by any resolution or commitment purportedly made in its name by the promoters of the coalition. The post 2027: We’re not joining your opposition coalition, PDP tells Lukman appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Santé : décès du Dr Abdou Cissé, directeur de l’hôpital d’Ourossogui
items.description: Le directeur de l’hôpital d’Ourossogui, dans la région de Matam, le docteur Abdou Cissé, a succombé à ses blessures le vendredi 20 novembre 2026, à la suite d’un accident de la circulation du mois d'octobre dernier à Ndioum. L’annonce a été faite samedi, par le ministre de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique. « Le ministère de la Santé et de l'Hygiène publique a la profonde tristesse d'annoncer le rappel à Dieu du Dr Abdou CISSÉ, survenu le 20 novembre 2026, des suites de l'accident de la circulation du mois d'octobre dernier à Ndioum », informe la tutelle à travers un communiqué publié samedi. D’après la tutelle, l’accident est survenu lors du retour du Dr Cissé, de la cérémonie de lancement d’Octobre Rose à Ndioum. Il convient de relever selon la tutelle que le Dr Abdou Cissé a consacré sa carrière au service public hospitalier avec engagement et dévouement. Au cours de son parcours professionnel, il a occupé plusieurs postes de responsabilité au sein du système hospitalier sénégalais. items.title: Université Norbert Zongo : Sawadogo T. Roger décroche son doctorat avec la mention Très honorable
items.description: L'Université Norbert Zongo de Koudougou compte un nouveau docteur en économie appliquée. Sawadogo T. Roger a soutenu sa thèse de doctorat ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026 à Koudougou. Intitulée « Essais sur le financement bancaire des économies de l'Union économique et monétaire ouest-africaine (UEMOA) », sa recherche a été validée par le jury avec la mention très honorable. Une distinction accueillie dans une ambiance de joie par ses collègues, amis et membres de sa famille. Pendant une dizaine de minutes, l'impétrant a présenté les résultats de ses travaux de recherche consacrés aux contraintes qui entravent l'accès au financement des économies de l'UEMOA. Trois principaux enseignements ressortent de son étude. D'abord, la concentration du secteur bancaire et le niveau de concurrence influencent les taux d'intérêt appliqués aux entreprises. Ensuite, les banques disposent de possibilités de refinancement auprès de la Banque centrale des États de l'Afrique de l'Ouest (BCEAO), contrairement à certaines perceptions faisant de celle-ci un facteur de limitation du financement. Enfin, la stabilité politique et sécuritaire apparaît comme un élément déterminant dans l'appréciation des risques par les banques et leur capacité à financer le secteur privé. L'impétrant a brillamment défendu son travail À l'issue de sa présentation, les membres du jury ont procédé à une analyse critique du document, formulé des observations et adressé plusieurs questions au candidat, qui a apporté des réponses satisfaisantes. Des recommandations lui ont également été faites en vue d'améliorer la qualité de son travail. Directeur de thèse du désormais docteur, le professeur titulaire Mahamadou Diarra a salué la pertinence et l'actualité du sujet, notamment au regard des difficultés de financement des économies africaines et du secteur privé. Il a également apprécié l'engagement du candidat dans le processus de recherche. Mahamadou Diarra, Directeur de thèse Selon lui, SAWADOGO T. Roger s'est montré particulièrement réceptif aux observations formulées tout au long de son parcours. Une grande partie des recommandations des trois rapporteurs ayant été prise en compte, son directeur de thèse y voit la preuve de son dévouement et de sa passion pour la recherche en sciences économiques. Visiblement heureux de cette consécration après plusieurs années de travail, le nouveau docteur a exprimé sa reconnaissance à son directeur de thèse, qui l'a accompagné et encouragé depuis ses premières années de formation, ainsi qu'à l'ensemble des professeurs ayant pris part à la délibération. Une vue des membres du jury Au terme des échanges, le jury a prononcé la validation de la thèse avec la mention très honorable. Une annonce qui a déclenché des cris de joie dans la salle, consacrant ainsi une nouvelle étape dans le parcours académique de SAWADOGO T. Roger, désormais docteur en économie appliquée de l'Université Norbert Zongo. Pr CHABOSSOU Augustin Foster C., Président du jury, Professeur titulaire en économie du développement à l’Université d’Abomey-Calavi (Bénin).Pr DIARRA Mahamadou : Directeur de thèse, Professeur titulaire en politique économique à l’Université Norbert-Zongo du Burkina Faso. Dr METOIOLE SOMÉ Dommbévin Juste, Rapporteur, Maître de conférences agrégé en sciences économiques à l’Université Norbert-Zongo. Dr KINDA Mohamed Tidjane , Rapporteur, Maître de conférences agrégé en économie du développement à l’Université Joseph-Ki-Zerbo. Dr DIANDA Issa , Examinateur, Maître de conférences agrégé en économie du développement à l’Université Nazi-Boni. Ces cinq universitaires ont constitué le jury chargé d'évaluer les travaux de recherche du doctorant sur le financement bancaire des économies de l'UEMOA. Minute.bf

items.title: UGEL cannot hide behind UG’s autonomy to evade Rent Commissioner – Appiagyei-Atua
items.description: Professor at the University of Ghana School of Law, Kwadwo Appiagyei-Atua, has challenged the University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL) to submit its accommodation charges to legal scrutiny. He argued that the company cannot rely on the university’s institutional autonomy to evade the authority of the Rent Commissioner. He maintains that UGEL is a legally distinct private entity, separate from the University of Ghana, and therefore cannot invoke the university’s academic freedom as grounds for resisting the Rent Commissioner’s jurisdiction over its rental premises. “Institutional autonomy cannot protect UGEL because it is a private entity, registered as being distinct and separate from UG,” he stated. Prof. Appiagyei-Atua argued that institutional autonomy, which is closely associated with academic freedom, cannot be used as a blanket protection for the company, particularly when its operations involve the provision of accommodation to students. He also raised concerns about a potential conflict of interest arising from the university’s Pro Vice-Chancellor serving as chairperson of the UGEL board. According to him, the arrangement raises questions about the university’s responsibility to protect students’ welfare while overseeing a company whose accommodation charges have become the subject of protests. The law professor contended that excessive accommodation charges undermine students’ academic freedom by creating conditions that make it difficult for them to access and fully participate in university education. He cited reports of students sleeping in classrooms and chapels or travelling long distances to attend lectures because of accommodation difficulties. “Charging cut-throat rates that force students to sleep in classrooms, chapels and travel long distances to school violates their academic freedom,” he said. He stressed that academic freedom should not be understood narrowly as a privilege enjoyed only by university management but must also protect students whose ability to pursue their education could be affected by unaffordable accommodation. He added that even if UGEL were considered part of the university, institutional autonomy could not justify actions that undermine the rights of members of the academic community. Appiagyei-Atua backs student protests Prof. Appiagyei-Atua also criticised the University of Ghana’s handling of the students’ campaign, accusing the institution of compromising its autonomy by allowing national security personnel to become involved in the matter without an invitation. He further alleged that the university had taken steps to intimidate the Graduate Students’ Association of Ghana (GRASAG), the Students’ Representative Council (SRC) and students seeking to demonstrate against the accommodation situation. He observed that GRASAG and the SRC had initially become reluctant to sustain the campaign, while concerned students continued their civil disobedience actions. Their persistence, he said, had helped bring the two student bodies back into the campaign, with the National Union of Ghana Students (NUGS) also joining the broader call. The professor urged the student leadership to remain united and sustain pressure on the university and UGEL, insisting that their demands were legitimate and reflected the interests of the wider academic community. UTAG urged to defend students’ rights Prof. Appiagyei-Atua also called on the University Teachers Association of Ghana (UTAG) to move beyond its traditional focus on the welfare and interests of lecturers and take a more active role in defending students’ rights. He argued that lecturers had a responsibility to speak up for vulnerable members of the university community, particularly students whose concerns might otherwise go unheard. “It’s time it turned away from its inward-looking approach informed by its welfarist, unionist approach to becoming human rights defenders, a voice for the voiceless on campus and in the larger society,” he said. He emphasised that students constitute approximately 80 per cent of the university’s academic community and should therefore be central to decisions affecting the institution. “Without you there’ll be no university and all lecturers will be made redundant,” he added. Prof. Appiagyei-Atua urged students and their representative bodies to remain resolute in pursuing their demands, stressing that accommodation arrangements at the university must respect students’ rights and comply with the legal protections governing rental properties.

items.title: I will deploy 2,000 ‘yellow yellow’ task force officers to check rent abuses in 2027 – Rent Commissioner
items.description: Acting Rent Commissioner Frederick Opoku says the Rent Control Department plans to deploy 2,000 task force officers across the country in the first quarter of 2027 to enforce provisions of the Rent Act. The move is expected to address widespread practices involving landlords demanding one, two or more years of rent in advance, despite the statutory restrictions on advance rent payments. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, he indicated that the planned task force, which he informally referred to as the “yellow-yellow” team, would visit households and investigate landlords suspected of violating the Rent Act. “Next year, I want to deploy 2,000 task force, yellow-yellow, that I call them, to go to the households and to begin to ask questions: You are in breach of Section 25(5) of the Act. Come and explain to rent control why you should not be prosecuted,” he said. His comments follow questions about the department’s progress in enforcing the Rent Act, particularly provisions requiring landlords to seek the appropriate approval before increasing rent and restricting advance rent payments. Mr Opoku said the department was currently prioritising public education and engagement with landlords and hostel operators ahead of a nationwide enforcement exercise. He disclosed that he had engaged hostel operators in Accra on July 5, 2026, through both physical and online meetings to explain the legal requirements governing rent increases and accommodation charges. He said he had also organised a separate engagement with landlords in November to educate them on their obligations under the law. Mr Opoku explained that the department had adopted a gradual approach because of the numerous challenges confronting the rental sector and the need to address them systematically. “I have not enforced anything, but I have to do. I cannot do all at a time,” he said. Mr Opoku, however, said the department intends to move beyond education to enforcement in the first three months of 2027.

items.title: Rent Control registers 3,000 landlords in Greater Accra in three months – Commissioner
items.description: The Acting Rent Control Commissioner, Frederick Opoku, says the Rent Control Department has registered about 3,000 landlords in the Greater Accra Region within the last three months as part of efforts to formalise Ghana’s rental sector and strengthen regulation. He disclosed that the registrations were carried out through a pilot exercise at the department’s Greater Accra office, forming part of internal reforms aimed at improving landlord identification, accountability and service delivery. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 21, Mr Opoku said the exercise was intended to address longstanding gaps in the department’s operations and ensure that landlords and tenants complied with existing legal requirements. “When I started the pilot registering, I have registered about 3,000 landlords in only Greater Accra office in the last three months,” he said. He explained that the registration drive was part of measures to ensure the department had reliable records of landlords and could verify their status when they sought assistance or lodged complaints. Mr Opoku said the department had also introduced stricter requirements for handling complaints, directing that landlords must first register with Rent Control before their grievances could be entertained. Tenants, he added, would be required to produce their rent cards as proof of their tenancy. According to him, some provisions of the law governing rental arrangements had not been enforced over the years, creating gaps in the system that his administration was seeking to address. The registration exercise forms part of broader reforms at the department, including plans to digitise its operations within the first three months of 2027. Under the proposed digital system, landlords and tenants will be able to access and download tenancy agreements online and complete them through a coded verification process. Mr Opoku said the reforms were intended to improve the department’s efficiency and ensure that Ghanaians received professional services.
